title_en: Wealthy People Are Hiding in Plain Sight (ft. Owen Zidar) | #428
title_zh: 富人就藏在眼皮底下（ft. Owen Zidar）｜#428
subtitle_zh: 普林斯顿经济学者 Owen Zidar 用税务全样本数据揭示：美国的典型富人藏在不起眼的私营企业里，也藏在政治与税制的细节里。
summary_zh: 本期 Rational Reminder（第428期）由 Ben Felix 与 Cameron Passmore 对话 Princeton 大学经济学与公共事务教授 Owen Zidar，《The Everywhere Millionaire》一书合著者。Zidar 借助与美国财政部合作十年、覆盖每一家私营企业的税务全样本数据，颠覆了人们对富人的想象：典型的美国有钱人并非 Elon Musk 或 Taylor Swift，而是经营着不起眼私营企业的普通企业主——汽车经销商、饮料分销商、承包商，甚至移动厕所的拥有者。数据显示，收入前0.1%人群中，来自私营企业的经营性收入占比从1960年的17%升至2022年的43%，同期工资占比降至35%；若把私营企业贡献固定在1980年代中期水平，Piketty 与 Saez 那张著名前1%收入份额U形图的涨幅将缩水一半。这些无处不在的百万富翁更像主街（Main Street）而非华尔街（Wall Street），仅约20%的收入来自金融与房地产。Zidar 强调发家致富靠的是拥有（ownership）而非打工，并解释转嫁实体（pass-through）如何成为顶层收入繁荣的核心。是一集用硬数据重绘美国财富地图的深度对话。
description: Wealthy People Are Hiding in Plain Sight (ft. Owen Zidar) | #428

turns.en: The way you get rich is by owning, not earning. We have some of the coolest data that's ever been assembled on the rich in America. She told me for herself, she said, if I could give my daughter $40 million or zero, I would give her zero.
turns.zh: 发家致富靠的是拥有（ownership），而不是打工赚钱。我们掌握了有史以来关于美国富人最酷的数据。她跟我掏心窝子说：如果可以给女儿4000万美元或者给0，她宁愿给0。

turns.en: Welcome to episode 428 of the Rapture Reminder Podcast. I'm Ben Felix, Chief Investment Officer at PWL Capital. And I'm Cameron Passmore, Chief Executive Officer at PWL Capital.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Rational Reminder 播客第428期。我是 Ben Felix，PWL Capital 的首席投资官。我是 Cameron Passmore，PWL Capital 的首席执行官。

turns.en: Today, Ben, we were joined by Owens Adar, Professor of Economics, Financial Researcher, and co-author of the book, The Everywhere Millionaire.
turns.zh: Ben，今天陪伴我们的是 Owen Zidar，经济学教授、实证研究者，也是《The Everywhere Millionaire》一书的合著者。

turns.en: Owens, Professor of Economics and Public Affairs at Princeton. In the episode, we talk about the unglamorous industries behind most fortunes, what the inequality debate misses, and how the rich spend their money and their time.
turns.zh: Owen 是普林斯顿大学经济学与公共事务教授。在这期节目里，我们聊聊大多数财富背后那些不起眼的行业、不平等讨论忽略了什么，以及富人如何花钱、如何花时间。

turns.en: Super interesting. Super interesting. And as always, stick around to the end to hear our thoughts about the conversation with Owen. But for now, let's get into the episode.
turns.zh: 太有意思了，太有意思了。照例，请听到最后，听我们聊聊与 Owen 对话后的感想。现在，让我们进入正片。

turns.en: Owens Adar, welcome to the Rapture Reminder Podcast. Thanks for having me. Owen, what's wrong with the common perception of what it means to be wealthy?
turns.zh: Owen Zidar，欢迎收听 Rational Reminder 播客，感谢你来做客。Owen，人们对财富的普遍认知错在哪里？

turns.en: Most people think that the way you get rich is to be like Elon Musk or Jamie Dimond or Taylor Swift. When you look in the data, that's just not actually at all who the typical rich person is in America.
turns.zh: 大多数人以为发财就得是 Elon Musk、Jamie Dimon 或 Taylor Swift 那样。但一看数据，这根本不是美国典型有钱人的样子。

turns.en: They're often ordinary business owners who've gotten extraordinarily rich, running unglamorous private businesses. So I have three young kids, and so I read a lot of kids' books, and we've half-jokingly talked about writing the ABCs of getting rich for the children's market.
turns.zh: 他们往往是做了了不起的财富的普通企业主，经营着不起眼的私营企业。我有三个小孩子，所以读很多童书，我们还半开玩笑地想过给童书市场写一本《发财ABC》。

turns.en: It's like A, for auto dealer, B, for beverage distributor, and C, for contractor. They're pretty mundane businesses, but when you have the opportunity like us to work with the Treasury to the full map of wealth in America, it's just very different because people don't answer surveys, unless you have investigative journalists or a celebrity following, you're just not gonna see the vast majority of private companies
turns.zh: A 是 Auto Dealer（汽车经销商），B 是 Beverage Distributor（饮料分销商），C 是 Contractor（承包商）。这些生意听起来很平凡，但当你有我们这样的机会与财政部合作、看到美国财富的全景图，就会发现完全是另一回事。因为人们不会回答调查问卷，除非你是调查记者或者有大牌光环，

turns.en: that don't have to file quarterly to investors. Can you talk about why that's important for people to understand? Yes, there are two key reasons.
turns.zh: 否则你永远看不到绝大多数私营公司——它们不需要向投资者提交季报。你能说说为什么这一点值得大家理解吗？可以，主要有两个原因。

turns.en: One is if you wanna get rich yourself. I think these everywhere millionaires provide a roadmap for success in America. And the second is if you wanna understand the economy and influence, these folks are really central characters in the saga of rising inequality in America.
turns.zh: 一是如果你自己也想发财。我认为这些'无处不在的百万富翁'提供了一张在美国取得成功的路线图。二是如果你想理解经济和影响力，这些人在美国不平等不断上升的大戏里其实是核心角色。

turns.en: So interesting. Let me see you think about it. I listened to the podcast a while ago with Mike Rowe. Do you remember the show Dirty Jobs? No, but I know the title, but I think that's in the right vicinity.
turns.zh: 真有意思。说说你怎么看这件事。我前阵子听了一期 Mike Rowe 的播客，你记得《Dirty Jobs》那个节目吗？不记得，但我知道这个标题。不过我觉得方向差不多。

turns.en: He did the show where he would go and kind of spend the day with people that did really dirty, like people cleaning sewers and stuff like that.
turns.zh: 那个节目里他会花一天时间跟干很脏活儿的人在一起，比如清理下水道之类的人。

turns.en: And he talked about how a ton of those people you would never know from watching the show, but a ton of those people were very wealthy because they own these types of businesses.
turns.zh: 他说很多人光看节目根本想不到，其实非常有钱，因为他们拥有这类生意。

turns.en: That's spot on. It's funny, our neighbor is like talking about turning this into a documentary and he puts the first clip together. And one of the things he shows of going from like the great Gatsby, Leonardo DiCaprio and a nice scene from the show Billions.
turns.zh: 完全正确。有意思的是，我家邻居正在说要把这个拍成纪录片，他还剪出了第一个片段。片段里有个镜头，是从《了不起的盖茨比》里 Leonardo DiCaprio 的漂亮场景、

turns.en: And he goes right to Porter Potties. And it's just like this guy who owns 100 Porter Potties and you know, think about all the big events, like all the races and Toronto has a big marathon.
turns.zh: 还有《Billions》剧里的场景，直接切到 Porter Potties，就是移动厕所。有个人拥有100个移动厕所。想想那些大型活动，各种比赛，多伦多有大型马拉松，

turns.en: You name the thing and someone needs to get Porter Potties there and clean them. And turns out that's a pretty good business if you have it at some scale.
turns.zh: 随便说个活动，都得有人把移动厕所运到现场再清理干净。结果发现只要做到一定规模，这是门相当不错的生意。

turns.en: Sure is. How was the source of income with the very top chains over the past century? Yeah, it's quite interesting to watch the rise of entrepreneurial income from private business.
turns.zh: 确实是。过去一个世纪里，最顶层人群的收入来源是怎么演变的？是的，看私营企业的创业性收入如何崛起，非常有意思。

turns.en: If you look at top 0.1% of income, I'll give you a few numbers. So in 1960, 17% of that income came from entrepreneurial income from business owners and almost twice that came from wages.
turns.zh: 如果把收入前0.1%的人群拿出来看，我给你几个数字。1960年，他们收入的17%来自企业主的经营性收入，来自工资的部分几乎是它的两倍。

turns.en: If you go to 2022, 43% came from private business and only 35% came from wages. And so you've seen this big rise in the share of income, especially at the top from private business.
turns.zh: 到了2022年，43%来自私营企业，工资只占35%。所以收入中来自私营企业的份额，尤其在顶层，出现了大幅上升。

turns.en: So that's another reason why I think this is quite important. One way to quantify that is to think about one of the most famous graphs in economics.
turns.zh: 这也是我认为它很重要的另一个原因。量化它的办法之一，是想想经济学里最有名的那张图之一。

turns.en: So Tomah Piketty and Emmanuel Syus had this famous U-shape top 1% graph where over the 20th century, they plot the share of income going to the top 1%.
turns.zh: Thomas Piketty 和 Emmanuel Saez 那张著名的前1%收入占比的U形图，画的是整个20世纪流向最富1%人群的收入份额。

turns.en: And if you do that same plot, but hold fixed the contribution of private business and mid 1980s, you only get half the rise in the top 1%. And so that's another way of accounting for how big this is, more than half of the rise of that famous top 1% share.
turns.zh: 如果你画同一张图，但把私营企业的贡献固定在1980年代中期的水平，前1%份额的涨幅就只有原来的一半。这是理解它有多重要的另一种方式——那张著名的前1%份额图里，超过一半的涨幅来自这里。

turns.en: Why is the common discourse about inequality incomplete? I mean, some of it is we just have had bad data. If you can't measure it, it's just not gonna be very salient, but that's completely an odds with what people see if you start to think about it.
turns.zh: 为什么关于不平等的常见讨论是不完整的？我理解一部分原因是我们一直没有好数据。测不到的东西就不会显眼。但这其实和你稍微留意一下就能看到的现象完全矛盾。

turns.en: So go to any nice golf resort or nice lake or nice mountain town and ask who owns the big houses and just go and ask them, what do you do? How did you make your money?
turns.zh: 你去任何一家高档高尔夫度假村、漂亮的湖边或者山城小镇，问问那些大房子是谁的，直接问他们：您是做什么的？钱是怎么赚来的？

turns.en: And it's a lot of mundane things. Like, oh, this guy owns seven Jiffy lubes or this guy distributes toilet paper for regional restaurants or this guy sells door handles.
turns.zh: 答案大多是些很平凡的事。比如，这人开了七家 Jiffy Lube（快修换油店），这人给区域餐馆分销厕纸，这人卖门把手。

turns.en: And it's some of those dirty jobs that you talked about that turns out to be what you see in the data. So some of it was just, we had this really unique opportunity to get a decade of work with the treasury where we could see every private business in America.
turns.zh: 就是你提到的那种'脏活儿'，数据显示确实如此。所以一部分原因只是我们以前没有好数据。我们有一次非常难得的机会，与财政部合作做了十年，能看到美国每一家私营企业。

turns.en: And that's what really shined the light on this hidden world of everywhere millionaires. So cool. Is the typical millionaire more Main Street or Wall Street?
turns.zh: 正是这一点照亮了'无处不在的百万富翁'这个隐秘世界。太酷了。你觉得典型的百万富翁更像是主街（Main Street）还是华尔街（Wall Street）？

turns.en: It's definitely more Main Street. So we added up all top 0.1% income of these private business owners and only about 20% comes from finance and real estate.
turns.zh: 绝对更像主街。我们把前0.1%收入里这些私营企业主的收入加总，只有大约20%来自金融和房地产。

turns.en: The majority come from every other industry, construction, healthcare, you name it. We're mostly a service economy. And another interesting thing is that it's in every town.
turns.zh: 大多数来自其他所有行业：建筑、医疗，凡是你能想到的。我们大体上是服务经济。还有个有意思的点是，每个城镇都有。

turns.en: So if you plot population, there's a pretty good job of predicting where you'll have a lot of the profits throughout the country. Whereas if you think it's just Wall Street, everything's happening in California, New York, and Silicon Valley, and New York, it's just not the case empirically.
turns.zh: 如果你把人口画出来，它能相当好地预测哪里会有一批这样的赚钱大户。要是你以为都是华尔街那套，事情都发生在加州、纽约、硅谷和纽约，经验数据上根本不是这样。

turns.en: Can you talk more about the industries that typically make the Main Street millionaires? I told you the ABCs. So if we tabulated by four digit sector, all of the top industries, and there's some white collar ones or the white collar ones are like law firms.
turns.zh: 你能再讲讲造就主街百万富翁的典型行业吗？我前面说了ABC。如果我们按四位数行业代码把所有头部行业列出来，有些是白领行业，白领行业里的代表是律所。

turns.en: There are a ton of lawyers in America. Collectively, they make more than $100 billion in top-owned firms and dentists and doctors. You see that type.
turns.zh: 美国律师特别多。他们合计在顶级律所里赚到超过1000亿美元，牙医、医生也是这类。

turns.en: But then there's a lot of really niche things like miscellaneous parts manufacturing. Auto dealers show up pretty high in their construction, architects, a lot of skills, service providers.
turns.zh: 但也有很多非常细分的行当，比如'杂项零部件制造'。汽车经销商排名相当靠前，还有建筑业、建筑师，各类技能型服务提供商。

turns.en: It's a range of really small things that you don't really see. But when you look at other data sets that we bought, so we bought private jet data, we bought private yacht data, and you see tons of interesting people coming in, like people who own convenience stores.
turns.zh: 都是些很小的、你平时看不到的行当。但你看看我们买的其他数据集——我们买了私人飞机数据、私人游艇数据——就会发现形形色色的有趣人物，比如开便利店的人。

turns.en: So there's this one guy that we talk about in the book, Beaver Applin, who owns a chain of convenience stores called Buckeys in the South, kind of in rural Texas.
turns.zh: 书里讲到一个人，Beau Cumins，他在南方、德州乡下一个地方拥有一连串叫 Buc-ee's 的便利店。

turns.en: And so if you haven't been to Texas or Louisiana, you might not have heard about this guy, but these things are like football field sized. Everything's bigger in Texas.
turns.zh: 如果你没去过德州或者路易斯安那，可能没听说过这个人，但那些店有橄榄球场那么大。德州什么都大。

turns.en: I went to high school in Texas. It's very much true of these convenience stores. There's people who make millions selling Buckeys merchandise like secondhand online.
turns.zh: 我在德州读的高中，这些便利店确实如此。还有人靠二手转卖 Buc-ee's 周边商品就能年入百万。

turns.en: And that's just not the image that normally comes to mind when you think about who's really rich. Who is the typical business owner? One thing that emerges from the data is that it's typically a white male who's in their 60s.
turns.zh: 这根本不是人们想到谁最有钱时脑子里通常浮现的形象。典型的企业主是谁？数据里显现的一个画像是：通常是六十岁上下的白人男性。

turns.en: And one of the reasons why is it takes decades to earn that much money. The Silicon Valley can move fast and break things, make money, make some app and get rich insanely fast.
turns.zh: 原因之一是要赚到那么多钱需要几十年。硅谷那套可以'快速行动、打破常规'，做个应用就暴富，快得离谱。

turns.en: It's just not the bottle. That's not the typical business owner. It often takes a lot of rolling up your sleeves, decades of grinding it out, concentrated ownership, a few owners, reinvestment.
turns.zh: 但那不是常态，那不是典型企业主。往往要卷起袖子苦干几十年，股权高度集中，少数几个股东，不断把利润再投入。

turns.en: And that's why you see them often in their 60s or 70s because they've been doing it their whole life. And they started with one store and then maybe two stores and then they just did slowly growing over time.
turns.zh: 所以你看到他们常常六七十岁了，因为这辈子都在干这个。从第一家店开始，然后也许第二家，慢慢做，随时间一点点长大。

turns.en: Yeah, the concentrated wealth thing is so interesting because we talk about this too. We talk about the benefits of diversification when you're investing, but to get to the next level of wealth, it really does often take that concentration.
turns.zh: 对，'财富集中'这点特别有意思，我们也常聊这个。我们做投资讲分散化的好处，但要跨到财富的下一个台阶，往往真的需要集中。

turns.en: And that's riskier. Don't get me wrong, that's certainly an aspect to it. But one thing that's pretty interesting is that we, not only in a series of research papers that the book is based on, tracked all their wealthy people.
turns.zh: 而那是更冒险的。别误会，这确实是其中一个方面。但有件事挺有意思：我们不仅在一系列研究论文——也就是这本书的基础——里追踪了所有富人，

turns.en: We also tracked everyone who's starting. So say like take every single entrepreneur, there's 10 million of them who started a business since 2000 and see how well they do accounting for the fact that this is risky, including all the people who flame out and get a zero.
turns.zh: 还追踪了每一个开始创业的人。比如把2000年以来创办企业的每一位创业者都拿出来，大约1000万人，看他们做得怎么样，并且考虑到这是有风险的，把所有干砸了、颗粒无收的人也算在内。

turns.en: And on average, they make a lot more money. I think it's like 18K more. The median person also makes more money by 5K and like often you see the people who fail don't actually fail in a sense that they'll get a job basically doing what they were doing before with not that big of a hit financially.
turns.zh: 平均而言他们赚得多得多，我记得大概多18K；按中位数也算多5K。而且你会发现失败的人其实并没有真正'失败'——他们基本还是干原来那一行找了份工作，财务上并没有受多大损失。

turns.en: And so you get this big upside of the downside is actually not quite as bad just from a statistical point of view. It could be quite stressful, but the risk is a lot more upside when you look at the data on all entrepreneurs in America.
turns.zh: 所以你有一个很大的上行空间，而从统计角度下行其实没那么可怕。过程可能压力很大，但把美国所有创业者的数据放在一起看，上行远大于风险。

turns.en: Kind of makes sense I guess because if you go and start a business and you run it for a bit, even if it's not successful, you probably gain a lot of sales.
turns.zh: 我猜也说得通，因为如果你去创办一家企业，经营过一阵，哪怕不成功，你大概也学到很多技能。

turns.en: You can go work for somebody else using that expertise. So you do have that sort of downside hedge from your human capital that you build as you're trying to run your business.
turns.zh: 你可以带着这些经验去给别人打工。所以在经营企业的过程中积累的人力资本，本身就是对下行风险的一种对冲。

turns.en: Absolutely. In fact, one of my best friends, he had this great business. He raised tens of millions of dollars, had a great team, hired designers from Apple.
turns.zh: 完全正确。实际上，我最好的朋友之一，他有很棒的公司，融了几千万美元，团队很出色，还从 Apple 挖了设计师，

turns.en: They're building ready to deploy apartment buildings. And it just turned out that the macro factors worked against him and interest rates went up and no one was building large properties.
turns.zh: 做可以即插即用的装配式公寓楼。结果宏观环境跟他作对，利率上去了，没人再建大型物业。

turns.en: And so like even though he had a great team and a pretty good idea, it just wasn't gonna happen. And it turns out he shifted, now he's the COO of a very big private company because he learned how to run a complex organization.
turns.zh: 所以尽管他有顶级团队、不错的点子，这事还是没成。后来他转型了，现在是一家非常大的私营公司的 COO，因为他学会了如何运营一个复杂组织。

turns.en: And it's exactly like you said. Yeah, it's a really interesting point. Who is on track to reach the 1% of the income and wealth distribution?
turns.zh: 正如你所说的那样。对，这个点真的很有意思。谁有望进入收入和财富分布的前1%？

turns.en: It depends on what trajectory you want to take. But I think one of the things that really jumped out in that entrepreneur work is that people who start out in an industry where you're likely to become an entrepreneur 10 or 15 years down the line are much better suited to make that jump into being rich in their life.
turns.zh: 这取决于你走哪条路径。但我觉得在创业者研究里特别突出的一点是：那些起步于某个行业、而这个行业里的人十年十五年后大概率会自己创业的人，一生跨入富裕行列的可能性要大得多。

turns.en: You could imagine comparing two people, somebody who goes into auto repair or someone who goes into auto manufacturing. The auto repair guy, if you look at people who work in that industry early on in their career, they're way more likely to own something by the time they're 40 versus working for Ford or GF or one of these car companies, you're not likely to be an owner, even though they seem pretty similar
turns.zh: 你可以想象两个人，一个去做汽车维修，一个去汽车制造。做汽修的人，如果你看职业生涯早期就进入这个行业的人，到40岁时他们拥有自己资产的概率要高得多；而在 Ford 或 GM 这类车企打工，哪怕在二十来岁的人看来

turns.en: from the perspective of a 20-something. So if you're thinking about that as a parent, what advice to give to your kids or someone early on in their career, this early labor market domain expertise is really quite important for putting you on the track to own.
turns.zh: 这两份工作挺像的，你却不太可能成为所有者。所以如果你是站在父母的角度，想给孩子或者刚入行的年轻人一个建议：早期的劳动力市场领域经验（domain expertise）对把你送上'拥有'这条路真的非常重要。

turns.en: And then the second group is people mid-career who they're earning a salary. And the way you get rich is by owning, not earning, typically. So it's pretty hard to get rich getting a W-2, which is the tax form for wage payments.
turns.zh: 第二类是中年拿工资的人。而发家致富靠的是拥有，不是赚取，通常如此。所以靠 W-2（工资收入的报税表）发财相当难。

turns.en: So that's kind of the more intermediate answer, depending on when you're answering the question. Can you talk about how the wealthy spend their money?
turns.zh: 所以算是个中段的回答，取决于你在什么时候问这个问题。能聊聊富人是怎么花钱的吗？

turns.en: It's really hard to measure consumption of the wealthy in a systematic way. That's something that we wanted to do really well for the book and ultimately couldn't nail it systematically.
turns.zh: 系统性地测量富人的消费真的很难。这是我们做书时特别想做好、但最终还是没能系统搞定的事。

turns.en: You, there's a lot of anecdotes and there's a lot of conventional wisdom. So one view is the Millionaire Next Door book, which is his best-selling book from a few decades ago that was based on marketing data.
turns.zh: 市面上有大量轶事和大量固有观念。一种观点来自《邻家的百万富翁》（The Millionaire Next Door），那是几十年前基于市场调查数据的畅销书，

turns.en: And it really emphasized kind of the frugality of wealthy individuals. Like you can't tell that your neighbor is a millionaire because they're driving an ordinary car, they're kind of living within their means, they don't have a nice watch, et cetera.
turns.zh: 非常强调富人的节俭。你看不出你邻居是百万富翁，因为他开普通车、量入为出、连块好表都没有，如此等等。

turns.en: There's some truth to that in the stories that we collected by talking to people, like their periods and a lot of these everywhere millionaires' lives where they were just hustling, not really doing much, but then later in their life, they have a super yacht.
turns.zh: 从我们和人们交谈收集的故事里，这话也有些道理。很多这种无处不在的百万富翁，早年一段就在埋头苦干、不怎么享受生活，到了人生后段却拥有超级游艇。

turns.en: So it depends a little bit on when you're looking and there's certainly a lot of these folks in the private jet data and the super yacht data.
turns.zh: 所以要看你截取的是哪个阶段。而且在这些私人飞机数据和超级游艇数据里，确实有大量这样的人。

turns.en: And so I don't think the case is quite as clear that everyone's really frugal all the time among the rich. I think there is a mix. Another reason why it's hard to know is that wealthy people don't answer surveys.
turns.zh: 所以我不认为'富人都一直很节俭'这个说法站得住。我觉得是混合的。另一个难以确知的原因是，有钱人从来不回答问卷调查。

turns.en: And so it's just hard to measure this in a systematic way that we were comfortable saying, like here's the bottom line empirically, but that's what I can tell you from some anecdotes and relative to the conventional wisdom.
turns.zh: 所以很难用一种让我们放心下结论的系统方式测量它，没法说'实证上的底牌就是这样'。我只能把这些从轶事里得到的、相对于固有观念的判断讲给你听。

turns.en: Yeah, that's interesting though. What about time use? How do the wealthy spend their time? A lot of them work and they don't like hobbies. There's several stories, one woman we talked to, she found herself and she's like, I don't want to spend the next 10 years of my life playing tennis.
turns.zh: 那挺有意思的。时间使用呢？富人怎么花时间？他们很多人工作，不喜欢爱好。有好几个故事。我们聊过一位女性，她突然想明白了：我不想用接下来十年去打发网球。

turns.en: I like want to do something. And she started a frozen quiche business that really grew to some serious scale. She's called the queen of quiche.
turns.zh: 我想做点事情。然后她创办了一家冷冻乳蛋饼（quiche）生意，后来真做到了相当大的规模。人称'乳蛋饼女王'。

turns.en: Other people try to have hobbies, this guy named John Osher, he sold one of his businesses and tried to retire and just couldn't do it, couldn't sit still.
turns.zh: 也有人试着培养爱好。有位叫 John Osher 的人，卖掉了自己的一家公司想退休，根本做不到，坐不住。

turns.en: And then finally started another business that kind of built on what he had done before. So I think the first business was spin pops. It's like suckers that kind of rotate so that the kid can eat it.
turns.zh: 最后又开了一家新公司，还是建立在他之前的积累上。我记得他第一家公司是做 Spin Pops 的，就是一种会转的冰棒糖，

turns.en: And he had all these contacts with manufacturers in China. And then he realized that there's kind of this market by walking the halls of Walmart and figuring out there's this market for electric toothbrushes that don't cost $100.
turns.zh: 小孩吃着更好玩。他跟中国制造商有一大堆人脉。后来他在 Walmart 的货架间转悠，发现存在一个'不用花100美元的电牙刷'的市场。

turns.en: And he just used the same spin pop contacts in China to make a toothbrush that was affordable. He just has that itch. And so some of it, they work a lot.
turns.zh: 他就用做 Spin Pop 的那批中国供应商做出一款买得起的电牙刷。他天生手痒。所以这批人里，有些人是拼命工作的。

turns.en: And most people are not inherited owners of their family business. That's like a quarter of the people we're talking about. So most of them kind of grew this thing and their stories of one of the people we talked to was like, oh, I confused Tuesdays and Saturdays because that's all kind of the same to me.
turns.zh: 而且大多数人并不是继承家族企业的老板，在我们谈论的人群里那类只占大约四分之一。多数人是自己一手把生意做大的。我们聊过的一个人说，他把周二和周六搞混了，因为对我来说每天都一样。

turns.en: Now, not everyone is like that. One guy we talked to in the book, he said, you can either have fun during the week or fun during the weekend.
turns.zh: 当然也不是每个人都这样。书里我们写到的一个人说：你可以选择工作日开心，或者周末开心。

turns.en: He's like, I ran a paper storage business so I could have fun during the weekend. Paper storage business literally just stored important financial documents.
turns.zh: 他说，我经营一家纸质文档仓储公司，就是为了能周末开心。纸质文档仓储，说白了就是存放重要财务文件。

turns.en: We're gonna make sure it doesn't burn. That's safe and that's it. Can you talk a little bit about the data that the book is based on? Like you mentioned some treasury data.
turns.zh: 保证不烧掉、放在保险的地方，仅此而已。能聊聊这本书所依据的数据吗？你前面提到一些财政部的数据。

turns.en: You're talking about surveys. Can you for the benefit of listeners just talk a little bit about what the conclusions from the book are based on?
turns.zh: 你还提到调查。能不能替听众讲讲，书里的结论到底建立在什么之上？

turns.en: We have some of the coolest data that's ever been assembled on the rich in America. So in 2014, myself and Eric Swick who wrote the book along with Danny Yegan, we were all just graduated from our PhDs and the treasury brought us in to try to answer a kind of narrow question.
turns.zh: 我们拥有有史以来关于美国富人最酷的数据。2014年，我和 Eric Zwick，还有与我们一起写书的 Danny Yagan，我们都刚拿到博士学位，财政部把我们招进去回答一个相对窄的问题。

turns.en: How much tax do private business owners pay? And in exchange, we started building research projects on the full set of businesses in America.
turns.zh: 私营企业主到底交多少税？作为交换，我们开始基于全美所有企业构建研究项目。

turns.en: Some of the foundation is kind of a decade of work on top incomes, top wealth, entrepreneurship that have the full population of every single firm in America and every single person in America who files a tax return.
turns.zh: 基础是十年关于最高收入、最高财富和创业研究积累，覆盖美国每一家企业的全样本，和每一个报税的人的全样本。

turns.en: So that's like the underlying stuff. And then there are a bunch of insights that we've kind of put together through that. And for the book, we built on those findings to try to find individuals because you can't do that in the tax day that's de-identified and it's a felony to try to find individuals.
turns.zh: 这是底层的东西，由此沉淀出一系列洞见。而为了写书，我们在这些发现之上去定位具体个人——在去标识化的税务数据里这是做不到的，去识别个人是重罪。

turns.en: But what you can do is say, okay, I know if you cut by industry, auto dealers show up in the top group. So let's look at some auto dealers and trade publications or yacht data or data on expensive homes throughout America.
turns.zh: 但你可以这么做：我知道按行业切分会发现汽车经销商出现在顶层人群里，那就去行业刊物里看一些汽车经销商，或者游艇数据、全美豪宅数据。

turns.en: There's property deed records. So there's a whole wealth of other things that we have done, including interviewing people and reading memoirs.
turns.zh: 还有产权登记记录。所以我们做了大量其他工作，包括访谈当事人和阅读回忆录。

turns.en: And we've combined them to have stories and statistics in the book. And that's what all these conclusions are based on. Absolutely incredible.
turns.zh: 我们把故事和统计数字合到书里，所有结论就是这么来的。太了不起了。

turns.en: What key factors allow the wealthy to thrive? There are several things. So one is running a private business because that's the typical way you do it.
turns.zh: 让富人得以兴旺的关键因素有哪些？有几件事。一是经营私营企业，这是典型路径。

turns.en: And then there are some important macro forces that have contributed to their rise. So one is the decline in interest rates. In the turn of the 1970s to the 1980s, Paul Volcker was really wrestling with inflation to try to get inflation down.
turns.zh: 然后有一些重要的宏观力量推动了他们的崛起。一是利率下行。1970年代之交到1980年代，Paul Volcker 与通胀苦战，努力把它压下来。

turns.en: And then we entered this period called the Great Moderation where rates were much lower. And that really boosted valuations both of public equities, but also private equities.
turns.zh: 之后我们进入了所谓的'大缓和'（Great Moderation）时期，利率低了很多。这真的大幅抬升了估值，公开股票如此，私募股权也一样。

turns.en: You could borrow to invest much more easily. You could sell your company for more in the future profits of your business. And your eight, nine, 10 were more valuable in a discounted sense.
turns.zh: 你可以更容易地借钱投资；你未来可以把公司卖得更贵，因为你生意的未来利润——第八年、第九年、第十年——折现之后更值钱了。

turns.en: And so that was a huge boon to the wealthy. A second, there's been pretty substantial tax cuts for private business owners that have accumulated and snowballed over recent decades.
turns.zh: 所以这对富人是一笔巨大的红利。第二，过去几十年里针对私营企业主的减税层层累积、越滚越大。

turns.en: There's also deregulation. You could sell things across state lines. There's globalization. You could talk to some of the people that we did and hiring fewer people.
turns.zh: 还有放松管制。你可以跨州销售。还有全球化。你可以像我们访谈的一些人那样，少雇很多人。

turns.en: And there are kind of moves that allow business owners not only to grow the pie, but also to get a bigger slice of the pie. And so all of those things have contributed to wealth accumulation.
turns.zh: 这些变化让企业主不仅能做大蛋糕，还能切走更大的一块。所有这些都助推了财富积累。

turns.en: Did you find any common personality traits that the wealthy show when they're children? Yes. So one concise way to do it is they're smart and illicit.
turns.zh: 你发现富人在孩童时期有什么共同的性格特质吗？有的。一个简洁的说法是：又聪明又淘气。

turns.en: Kind of street smart, more so than academically smart. So one super interesting fact that we did in the entrepreneur work in the middle of the book was we linked all those 10 million entrepreneurs to their standardized test scores.
turns.zh: 是街头智慧那种聪明，而不是学业上的聪明。我们在书中间创业者部分做了一件特别有意思的事：把那1000万创业者全部链接到他们的标准化考试成绩。

turns.en: So that's the SAT and ACT. You can compare a general measure of success, like how much do you earn when you're 35 to how likely are you to start a star business, which means top 10% of revenue or employment.
turns.zh: 也就是 SAT 和 ACT。你可以拿一个通用的成功度量——比如35岁时你挣多少钱——去对比你创办一家明星企业（即收入或雇员数居前10%的企业）的可能性。

turns.en: And if you look at the standard measure of success across SAT scores, if you have the top score, you're gonna make 200K if you have a 1600. And if you have something close to the median, it's much lower, it's like 70 or 80K.
turns.zh: 如果你看SAT分数与这种标准成功度量的关系：考满分1600的人，能挣20万美元；分数接近中位数的人要低得多，大概7万到8万。

turns.en: Whereas if you look at the probability you're gonna do well as an entrepreneur, it's much flatter. Basically, there's not much of a difference between getting a median SAT score and a 1600 for the probability you start a star business.
turns.zh: 但如果看的是'作为创业者干出名堂'的概率，那条线平坦得多。基本上，SAT考到中位数和考到1600，对你创办明星企业的可能性差别不大。

turns.en: Another thing that jumped out is this illicit part. And so they're a little bit more likely to fight or get into trouble with the law, which is maybe related to kind of breaking conventions or pushing the envelope a bit.
turns.zh: 另一个跳出来的是'淘气'那部分。他们稍微更爱打架、或更可能有法律上的麻烦，这也许跟打破常规、挑战边界有点关系。

turns.en: That's a little more speculative, but that is something that shows up in the data that they have the higher probability of having had some run-ins before.
turns.zh: 这有点更推测性，但数据里确实显示：他们以前有过某种'擦枪走火'的概率更高。

turns.en: Interesting. I was thinking more risk seeking when you said that. Yeah, I mean, that also I think is related. Where do the wealthy go to college?
turns.zh: 有意思。你说的时候我想到的是更偏'寻求风险'。对，我觉得这也相关。富人都上什么大学？

turns.en: So most of these folks do go to college, but you don't have to go to an elite college to become an everywhere millionaire. There are many that didn't that we talked to.
turns.zh: 这些人大多数确实上了大学，但你不必上名校也能成为无处不在的百万富翁。我们访谈的人里就有很多没上过大学的。

turns.en: It's kind of all over and it really depends on the person. So I'm trying to think of some of the characters we have. So Dick Portillo, the hot dog billionaire, he didn't go to college, Karen Bentledge, the tanning bed and wax distribution leader, she didn't go to college.
turns.zh: 情况五花八门，真的因人而异。我在想书里的一些人物。做热狗生意的亿万富翁 Dick Portillo 没上过大学；做日光浴床和美容蜡分销的 Karen Bentledge 也没上过大学。

turns.en: Beaver Applin went to Texas A&M. Larry Miller, the auto dealer went to BYU. There are some who go to elite colleges and then end up trying to do this thing afterwards.
turns.zh: Beau Cumins 上了 Texas A&M。汽车经销商 Larry Miller 上了 BYU。也有人念了名校，毕业后转头来干这个。

turns.en: So like if you go to HBS or Harvard Business School or Stanford GSB or some of these other top business schools, there is this growing popularity and search funds where they basically want to raise money and go buy an HVAC company in Mississippi.
turns.zh: 比如你上了 HBS、哈佛商学院，或 Stanford GSB，或其他顶级商学院，现在 search funds（寻猎基金）越来越流行，他们基本上就是想募一笔钱，去密西西比买一家 HVAC（暖通空调）公司。

turns.en: It's not obvious you needed to go to Stanford to do that. You probably are benefited from the ability to raise funds and some of the skills you learned, but you could just go buy one of these companies.
turns.zh: 很难说做这个非得去斯坦福不可。融资能力和在那里学到的一些技能可能确实帮到你，但你完全可以自己去买这样一家公司。

turns.en: There's a case for doing that as well. Yeah, the access to capital thing is probably real though. Yeah, although one interesting thing that when we were looking at where entrepreneurs come from is that we found that early labor market experience and domain expertise was actually much more important empirically than access to capital and being wealthy right when you wanted to start the thing.
turns.zh: 这么做也有它的道理。对，资本可得性（access to capital）这一点估计是真的。嗯，不过我们研究创业者来自哪里时发现，一个有意思的点是：早期的劳动力市场经验和领域专长，在实证上比'启动时有钱、有资本'重要得多。

turns.en: And so the way we did that, so for the wealthy one, we compared early workers at IPO firms and so the basic thought experiment is take a guy who's like employee number four versus employee number 20.
turns.zh: 我们的做法是，就拿富人那一侧而言，我们比较了 IPO 公司的早期员工，基本思想实验是：找一个大概是4号员工的人，和20号员工比较。

turns.en: They're probably pretty similar people and just one got there earlier and number four has way more equity. And then after the IPO, how much more likely is employee four to go and found another company versus employee 20?
turns.zh: 这两个人大概率差不多，只是一个进得早，4号拿到了多得多的股权。那么 IPO 之后，4号员工再去创办一家新公司，比20号员工可能性高多少？

turns.en: He's got a lot more money. How much does money matter for future success? And we didn't see that money in that sample mattered that much. Even though there's a very sharp difference in how much money employee four, employee 20 half.
turns.zh: 他有钱得多。钱对未来的成功有多重要？在这个样本里，我们并没有看到钱有那么重要，尽管4号员工和20号员工之间的财富差距非常悬殊。

turns.en: So that's what that's based on. There's also some evidence based on lottery winnings. If you go in the US and look at people who've won lotteries, the probability of starting businesses isn't that different from lottery winners of big lotteries or small lotteries or no winnings at all.
turns.zh: 这就是那个结论的来源。还有一些基于彩票中奖的证据。在美国，看看中彩票的人，中大彩票、小彩票或者压根没中奖的人，创业的概率差别并不那么大。

turns.en: I do think capital matters in many cases, but it's surprisingly less important in the context we've studied than knowing how the business works.
turns.zh: 我确实认为资本在很多情况下很重要，但出人意料的是，在我们研究的语境里，它远不如'懂得这门生意怎么转'那么重要。

turns.en: Yeah, that's a very interesting. What factors explain which places foster upward mobility? Yeah, I think something we'd like to research a bit more.
turns.zh: 对，这很有意思。哪些因素解释了为什么有的地方更能促进向上流动？嗯，我觉得这是我们还想再多研究一点的。

turns.en: We have established some descriptive facts. So if you go across the country, there are places like Salt Lake City where you're three times likelier to start a business if you grew up there than in other parts the South.
turns.zh: 我们已经确立了一些描述性事实。比如在全国范围内，像盐湖城（Salt Lake City）这样的地方，如果你在那里长大，创业的可能性是美国南部一些地区的三倍。

turns.en: Right now we don't have a clear answer to that other than some speculation. So one thing that people say if you go to Salt Lake City, there's a substantial Mormon population in Salt Lake City and one of the things that's often a part of people's experience when they grow up in the Mormon community is proselytizing.
turns.zh: 目前我们对原因还没有明确答案，只有一些猜测。一种说法是，盐湖城有相当多的摩门教徒，在摩门教社区长大的经历里，很多人都会去传教。

turns.en: And so you have to go knock on doors, learn to deal with the persistence and grit of hearing no and saying that it. And I feel like that's something that contributes to successful entrepreneurship later on.
turns.zh: 你得挨家挨户敲门，学会面对被拒绝的坚持和韧劲，把'不'字咽下去。我感觉这有助于日后创业成功。

turns.en: Now, I don't know if that's really the thing, but that is one possible explanation seems somewhat plausible to me. Can you keep going on that and talk more about what explains the gaps in business creation across different population groups?
turns.zh: 当然我不确定这就是真正的原因，但它是一种可能的解释，对我来说也算说得通。你能顺着这个再往下讲讲吗？不同人群之间创业率的差距，背后是什么？

turns.en: There's all these different hypotheses for what might matter. It could be like access to capital, it could be how rich your parents were, it could be you have mentors, can you learn from people on how things work?
turns.zh: 关于什么因素重要，有各种各样的假说。可能是资本可得性，可能是你父母多有钱，可能是有没有导师，能不能从别人那里学到事情怎么玩。

turns.en: You can look at gaps across different groups. So for example, if you think it's all about money, then one puzzling thing that emerges from the data is the gap across men and women for founding.
turns.zh: 你可以看不同群体间的差距。比如说，如果你认为一切都取决于钱，那数据里有个费解的现象，就是男女创办企业之间的差距。

turns.en: Because if it's all about like having rich parents, men and women aren't systematically to poorer parents or richer parents, yet men are much more likely to start businesses than women in the data.
turns.zh: 因为如果靠的是父母有钱，男性并不比女性系统性地拥有更穷或更富的父母，可在数据里，男性创业的可能性远高于女性。

turns.en: It's also not about college attendance because recently women are way more likely to be college graduates than men. I mean, often in like admissions committees have to fight if they wanna make it 50-50 to kind of let in to more marginal men and test scores relative to women because women tend to be better students.
turns.zh: 这也不是上大学的问题，因为近年来女性大学毕业的比例远高于男性。常常是招生委员会要费劲才能做到50-50，为了录取更多成绩相对女性稍弱的边缘男性申请人，因为女性往往是更优秀的学生。

turns.en: There are some puzzles and then a few things jump out. One is the kids of business owners are way more likely to be business owners themselves.
turns.zh: 所以存在这些疑团，也有几个发现跳了出来。一个是企业主的孩子成为企业主的可能性大得多。

turns.en: You could drop all the ones that have a family firm. So it's not about staying in the family firm and the reason why you're gonna be a business owner is because you are just running what your parents gave you.
turns.zh: 你可以把所有继承家族企业的人剔除，所以不是'守摊子'——不是因为你要经营父母交给你的东西才成为企业主。

turns.en: It's something more about exposure to this entrepreneurial human capital that I think is an important part of what's going on. And so some of the places I also think they have more opportunity like flatter organizations where you can really see, hey, you know, I could do this myself or this is something that I could do that is where we are in terms of our current understanding of what's going on to explain those gaps.
turns.zh: 更多的是一种对'创业型人力资本'的接触和浸染，我觉得这是关键的一部分。另外有些机会更多的地方，比如层级更扁平的组织，你会觉得'哎，这事我也能干、这个我能做'。关于这些差距，我们目前的理解大致到这里。

turns.en: It makes sense when you think about if a kid grows up in that environment and sees their parent, whatever, doing entrepreneurial stuff and taking risks that they would be more likely and willing to do that and kind of know what steps to take.
turns.zh: 想想就合理：如果一个孩子在那种环境里长大，看到父母在做创业的事、承担风险，他就更可能也更愿意去做，并且大致知道该走哪几步。

turns.en: What do you think entrepreneurs need to be successful? Lots of things have to go right. So some of it is luck and some of it is some grit. It's amazing for a lot of these stories.
turns.zh: 你觉得创业者要成功需要什么？很多事情得同时顺。一部分是运气，一部分是韧劲。很多故事里都有那么一些时刻，眼看着就成不了了。

turns.en: There are a lot of times when it wasn't gonna work. The queen of quiche that I talked about, said her name's Nancy Mueller. She initially made quiche for Christmas parties which she froze them and that's what she did.
turns.zh: 我说过的乳蛋饼女王，她叫 Nancy Mueller。她最早是给圣诞派对做乳蛋饼，冷冻起来，就是这么起家的。

turns.en: And then she wanted to scale it up a little bit. And eventually it was getting to such a scale that she was fusing washing machines to dry spinach, which is kind of gross.
turns.zh: 后来她想扩大一点规模，最终大到什么程度呢，她用洗衣机来甩干菠菜，想想有点恶心。

turns.en: When you talk to her, her dad said something like, with each box of quiche you're sending to the store, you're like shipping dollars because she was making loss.
turns.zh: 跟她聊天时，她父亲说过类似这样的话：你每往商店发一箱乳蛋饼，就等于往里贴钱，因为她在亏本。

turns.en: She needed to have real scale to make enough. And there were decades when it wasn't really looking great. And then eventually she got a big store kind of like Costco or I think it was Price Chopper was the name of it at the time or like a Walmart that put in a big order.
turns.zh: 她必须真正上规模才能赚到钱。有好些年情况都不怎么样。直到后来一家大零售商，类似 Costco——我记得当时叫 Price Chopper——或者像 Walmart 那样的，下了一大笔订单。

turns.en: And then she finally got enough scale to really make it. But it was a long time. And so some of it is stick to it-iveness and really having a vision and having to pan out and also knowing when to exit.
turns.zh: 她这才拿到足够规模，真正做成了。但那是漫长的过程。所以一部分是坚持不懈、心中有蓝图并最终把它兑现，也包括知道什么时候该退出。

turns.en: So she was pretty nervous that if you just have this concentrated customer base they could leave. So she sold the business too, mostly worried about losing that big contract.
turns.zh: 她当时相当担心客户太集中，万一大客户走了就完了。所以她把企业卖掉了，主要就是因为怕丢掉那份大合同。

turns.en: How has the share of national income accruing to labor in the US changed over time? It's a striking thing to look at the labor share. I think it's really cratered nationally.
turns.zh: 美国国民收入中流向劳动的份额随时间如何变化？看劳动份额（labor share）是很震撼的。我觉得在全国范围内它真的塌陷了。

turns.en: And then if you focus by several points but if you focus on pass-through owners so these private business owners. So I guess I'll give you some broader macro facts if I can remember them off the top of my head then I'll talk about the labor share within pass-through.
turns.zh: 而且如果你聚焦于转嫁实体（pass-through）所有者，也就是这些私营企业主，虽然降了几个点，但我想先讲讲我大概还记得的宏观背景，然后再讲转嫁实体内部的劳动份额。

turns.en: Between 1990 and 2020, about 60% of the growth in value added which is profits plus wages of the business sector. So that's like traditional corporations, these private businesses, 60% of that has been in these private pass-through firms.
turns.zh: 1990年到2020年之间，商业部门增加值——利润加工资——的增长中，大约60%来自这些私营的转嫁实体企业，包括传统公司制企业和这些私营企业。

turns.en: And by pass-through I mean firms that don't face the traditional corporate tax but instead the profits and losses of the business flow through to the owners.
turns.zh: 所谓转嫁实体，是指不缴纳传统公司税的企业，利润和亏损直接转嫁到所有者个人税表上。

turns.en: And that's what's really been booming for the staff we were talking about before in terms of the top 1% share. Okay, so if you take all business activity and how big the pie is, the growth in the pie, 60% of that has been in pass-throughs.
turns.zh: 这正是前面说的前1%份额暴涨背后真正繁荣的部分。好的，那如果把所有商业活动、蛋糕的大小、蛋糕的增长拿出来看，其中60%的增长来自转嫁实体。

turns.en: And then there's the question, okay, how much does labor get and how much does capital get? One way to measure the pie just as like a labor productivity measure in 2030, $4,000 per worker was typical labor productivity.
turns.zh: 然后问题就变成：劳动拿多少，资本拿多少？衡量蛋糕的一种方式，比如按劳动生产率算：2030年，典型的劳动生产率是每位工人4000美元。

turns.en: And then by 2021, it went to $52,000 per worker. So that was an $18,000 per worker rise in labor productivity. And if that were evenly split between labor and capital that would be $9,000 each.
turns.zh: 到2021年，每位工人涨到52000美元。也就是说每位工人的劳动生产率涨了18000美元。如果这笔钱在劳动和资本之间平分，那应该是各得9000美元。

turns.en: But what you see in the data for these top-owned firms is that 15K goes to owners and only 3K went to workers. And so there was a very material decrease in the labor share.
turns.zh: 但你在这些顶级所有权企业的数据里看到的是，15K 流向了所有者，只有3K 流向工人。所以劳动份额出现了实质性的下降。

turns.en: So I think in 2000, it was something like two thirds went to labor. And then by 2014, it was like half and half. Part of the story of what's going on here is a material decline in the labor share.
turns.zh: 我想2000年时大概是三分之二归劳动，到2014年就差不多一半对一半了。这里正在发生的故事之一，就是劳动份额的大幅下降。

turns.en: Some of that is because owners are getting a bigger slice but it's also the pie is growing. There is some labor productivity growth. What does that development mean for the relationship between business owners and workers?
turns.zh: 一部分原因是所有者拿走了更大的一块，但同时也是蛋糕在变大，劳动生产率确实有所增长。这种变化对企业主和工人的关系意味着什么？

turns.en: It means that an important part of why wealthy business owners are doing well is because they've kept a larger share of the slice. Now, there are lots of things going on there.
turns.zh: 意味着富有的企业主过得好，一个重要原因是他们留住了更大的份额。这里面有很多因素在起作用。

turns.en: Some of this you could say, look, these are economic forces where expertise and ownership really matter. So one example I like to give in that is imagine someone like my former colleague, Kevin Murphy.
turns.zh: 你可以说，看，这是经济力量使然，专业能力和所有权真的重要。我举的一个例子是，想想我以前的同事 Kevin Murphy。

turns.en: He's an amazing economist. Somebody once joked his first language was economics. You could just go and like think about things and give you a really cogent explanation.
turns.zh: 他是了不起的经济学家。有人开玩笑说他的第一语言是经济学。你随便抛个问题，他就能给你一个非常透彻的解释。

turns.en: So he does a lot of consulting work and antidrust. And so imagine you're some big company, you wanna acquire another company and if you get Kevin to do it, he's gonna raise the probability this merger happens by 10%.
turns.zh: 他做很多咨询工作和反垄断方面的工作。想象你是某家大公司，想要收购另一家公司，如果请 Kevin 出马，他能让这笔并购成功的概率提高10%。

turns.en: This is a billion dollar deal. 10% of a billion dollar deal is really valuable. That's increasingly valuable over time as you get bigger and bigger companies and economic growth.
turns.zh: 这是一笔10亿美元的交易。10亿美元交易的10%是非常有价值的。而且随着公司越做越大、经济不断增长，这笔价值还在上升。

turns.en: And so Kevin getting a growing share of what's going on is not an unreasonable proposition. He's bringing a lot to the table. And so that's part of what's going on.
turns.zh: 所以 Kevin 在其中拿走越来越大的份额并不是不讲道理。他贡献了很多。这是正在发生的事情的一部分。

turns.en: Another part is this is more nefarious and it's about like a series of regulatory restrictions or things that prevent entry and competition and essentially pull up the drawbridge from other people trying to get rich in the same way that you're getting rich and exploiting that.
turns.zh: 另一部分就没那么好看了：一系列监管限制或者设置进入壁垒、阻碍竞争的东西，本质上是对想跟你一样发财的人吊起吊桥，然后从中渔利。

turns.en: It's hard to say that you have to kind of go by case by case to talk about what's actually going on. But there's definitely some of that as well.
turns.zh: 很难一概而论，得一个案子一个案子地看实际发生了什么。但这类事情肯定也存在。

turns.en: It's a nuanced picture for what's going on in the economy. And I think these things can happen at the same time. It both be true. It just depends on what industry and company you're looking at.
turns.zh: 经济里正在发生的事，图景很微妙。而且我觉得这些可以同时成立，两者都是真的，取决于你看的是哪个行业、哪家公司。

turns.en: How do non-competes impact workers? One striking fact about the economy is almost one in five workers have a non-compete. You can make the case for some proprietary things but for janitors or people making sandwiches it seems pretty tough to swallow.
turns.zh: 竞业禁止协议（non-compete）对工人有什么影响？经济里一个惊人的事实是，几乎五分之一的工人签有竞业协议。有些涉及专有技术的理由可以说得通，但清洁工、做三明治的人也签这个，就很难让人接受了。

turns.en: And what it does is it lowers wages because it makes it harder for them to move and get offers from elsewhere. And that's one of the forces that probably contributed to the developments I was just talking about of the labor share not moving up and workers not enjoying all that productivity growth that we've seen economy-wide.
turns.zh: 它的效果是压低工资，因为它让工人更难跳槽、更难拿到别的录用机会。这很可能就是劳动份额上不去、工人没能享受到全经济生产率增长的那些力量之一。

turns.en: Geez, I mean, it sounds like a rough picture that you're painting for labor. The labor share is at historic lows. There are a bunch of measurement issues related to it, one of which is the rise of passers.
turns.zh: 天哪，听起来你描绘的这幅图景对劳动者相当严峻。劳动份额处于历史低位。这里面有一堆测量问题，其中之一就是转嫁实体的崛起。

turns.en: But fundamentally, they're pretty material declines and just the share of the pie that goes to workers. How do you think that resolves over time or does it?
turns.zh: 但根本上，流向工人的那一份蛋糕确实出现了实质性下降。你觉得这会随时间如何演化？还是说无解？

turns.en: I think that's one of the main questions that we face as a society is can you continue to operate just without paying attention to it? And obviously you've had very tumultuous political environments and elections and people being very upset with the state of things.
turns.zh: 我认为这是我们社会面对的核心问题之一：能不能一直对它视而不见地运转下去？显然，政治环境非常动荡，选举激烈，人们对现状非常不满。

turns.en: Not just in the US, but just everywhere in the world that some of that could be a response to globalization and some of these forces where the share going to labor is not looking high or if you look at AI and some predictions people have, there's plausible scenarios or that's only going to accelerate.
turns.zh: 不只在美国，全世界都差不多。其中一部分可能就是对全球化等力量的回应——流向劳动的份额看起来并不高。再看看 AI 和人们的一些预测，有些情景是合理的：只会加速。

turns.en: I'm not a political scientist but it doesn't strike me as implausible that this will continue to be a very volatile situation and it's important to think about reasonable interventions that are good for economic growth and good for prosperity and capitalism that can make sure we don't sacrifice the ability to have a healthy economy and also make sure people get paid.
turns.zh: 我不是政治学家，但在我想来，这种动荡持续下去并不令人意外。重要的是思考一些合理的干预，既有利于经济增长、有利于繁荣和资本主义，确保我们不牺牲健康经济的能力，又能保证人们拿到应有的报酬。

turns.en: This is a tough question. I'm asking you to solve the world's problems quite literally but what are some examples? Like what could solve that?
turns.zh: 这个问题很难。我这简直是在请你解决世界难题，但能举几个例子吗？什么样的办法能起作用？

turns.en: One thing that's a little off topic but it's fine is the healthcare in the US were really unlike many other countries in terms of how we do it.
turns.zh: 有一件事有点跑题，但没关系：就是美国的医疗体系，我们的做法和许多其他国家真的很不一样。

turns.en: They're just absolutely crushing healthcare costs for small businesses. It's very bad for business and it's very bad for their workers. So I'm on the board of a daycare and this year we were quoted a health insurance cost increase of 50%, literally next year, whatever you're paying for health insurance for your employees goes up by 50%.
turns.zh: 医疗成本对小型企业来说简直是碾压性的。对企业很糟糕，对员工也很糟糕。我在一家日托中心做董事，今年我们拿到的健康保险报价涨幅是50%。字面意思是：明年，你为员工支付的健康保险费一律上涨50%。

turns.en: You're saying, okay, I'm gonna tell some set of workers who are devoting their life to helping kids who are basically making the minimum wage.
turns.zh: 你的意思是，好，我要告诉一群把职业生涯奉献给孩子的人——他们拿的基本是最低工资——

turns.en: I'm gonna take your $30,000 and then $7,000 that is no longer gonna go to you, it's gonna go to the health insurance company. That seems pretty crushing.
turns.zh: 我要从你的30000美元里再拿走7000美元，这笔钱不再归你，而是归保险公司。这看起来相当残酷。

turns.en: We have to figure out a way to do something about this and in a separate work we studied what is the effect of rising employer-sponsored health insurance costs on the labor market and one thing that it does is it makes the US a lot less competitive.
turns.zh: 我们必须想办法改变这一点。在另一项独立研究里，我们研究了雇主提供（employer-sponsored）的医疗保险成本上升对劳动力市场的影响。其中一个效应是，它让美国的竞争力大打折扣。

turns.en: It's hard to say I'm gonna go build a plant in Ohio if I have to pay $27,000 on top of whatever I pay that person wages to pay for a family plan.
turns.zh: 如果我必须为一份家庭保单额外支付27000美元，那我说'我要去俄亥俄建一座工厂'就很难了。

turns.en: I guess it's just not gonna be something that is gonna be reasonable relative to other production opportunities. So I think the fact that healthcare is so expensive in the US and growing so rapidly makes it tough to compete and makes it tough for somebody making low income to survive.
turns.zh: 我想相对其他生产机会来说，那根本划不来。所以我认为，医疗在美国如此昂贵、增长如此迅猛，让竞争变得艰难，也让低收入者难以生存。

turns.en: And so I think that this just has to change. So some economists who I really respect, Amy Finkelstein and Loran, I know if they have this book trying to remember what it's called something like we've got you covered but the basic idea is if you have an old house there are a couple of different strategies and the old house is the healthcare system.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得非变不可。有几位经济学家我非常尊敬，Amy Finkelstein 和 Loran，我不确定他们的书是不是叫《We've Got You Covered》之类的，基本想法是：如果你有一栋老房子，有几种不同的策略，老房子就是医疗体系。

turns.en: You can like try to rebuild things and tinker around and then their basic coin is like this is not a situation where you can just tinker with it, we need to tear down and you should just completely overhaul the thing.
turns.zh: 你可以试着翻修、这里敲敲那里补补。但他们的基本观点是：这种局面不是修修补补能解决的，得推倒重来，彻底改造。

turns.en: And what should you have? Something that's simple, basic and free. Simple meaning you don't have all these crazy institutions. Basic meaning it's kind of like the back of an airplane you're gonna pay to get from point A to point B but it might not be the most comfortable thing in the world.
turns.zh: 那应该建成什么样？简单、基础、免费。简单，是指不要有那么多乱七八糟的机构。基础，有点像经济舱：你付钱从A地到B地，但未必是世界上最舒服的体验。

turns.en: If you want a more comfortable version you have to pay more and free. Mainly you don't have all these deductibles and things because that empirically doesn't work as well as people might think.
turns.zh: 想要更舒服的版本，就得加钱。免费，主要是不要有那些免赔额之类的东西，因为经验数据表明它们的效果并不像人们以为的那么好。

turns.en: That's one example of a place to do it. And you know for small business owners if you're running a business and your costs go up by 50% on wages it's really hard to deal with that.
turns.zh: 这是一个可以动手的方向。要知道，对小企业主来说，如果你在经营一家企业，工资相关的成本上涨50%，真的很难应对。

turns.en: You can pass some of that on but if you're small you can't compete with a big firm that can self-insure and navigate some of this more effectively.
turns.zh: 你可以转嫁一部分，但如果你规模小，你就竞争不过那些能自保、能更高效应对这些的大公司。

turns.en: So I think it's also important for dynamism in the United States. Super interesting, you said that was a bit off topic but I thought it was great, really interesting stuff.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这对美国的（经济）活力也很重要。太有意思了，你说有点跑题，可我觉得特别棒，真的很有意思。

turns.en: How do inheritance is shape the path to wealth? Inheritance is a super interesting thing. So my co-author Eric, he's funnier than I am. He likes to joke.
turns.zh: 继承如何塑造通往财富的路径？继承是非常有意思的事。我的合著者 Eric 比我幽默，他爱开玩笑。

turns.en: He's like, that's his recommended path to getting registered. Just if you can inherit it, that's where you start. But it's very complicated.
turns.zh: 他说那就是他推荐的发财路径：能继承就先继承。但这件事非常复杂。

turns.en: In the book we tell a couple of different stories. Basically the story of it going well and the story of it going very poorly. The one where it goes well, they were very coordinated.
turns.zh: 书里我们讲了好几个不同的故事，有顺利的版本，也有非常糟糕的版本。顺利那一家，配合得非常好。

turns.en: The dad basically brought the son up, put him in hard jobs at the company. He was really learning the ropes. You're very smart about the transition during COVID when the value of the business cratered.
turns.zh: 父亲基本上是把儿子带出来的，安排他去公司干最苦的岗位，真正学门道。交接的时机也选得非常聪明，就在新冠期间企业价值暴跌的时候。

turns.en: That's when they handed it over because for tax purposes it was no longer eligible. It was below the exemption levels. That ended up working great.
turns.zh: 他们那时完成移交，因为从税务角度，企业价值已经低于免税额度，不再应税。结果非常成功。

turns.en: On the other hand, we told the story of a street sweeper repair business that had a couple of brothers, one of whom was somewhat responsible and put a lot of his money in.
turns.zh: 另一边，我们讲了一个街道清扫车维修公司的故事，家里几个兄弟，其中一个比较有责任感，往公司投了很多钱。

turns.en: The others treated it like a bank account. It was very contentious. The one brother was really a financial risk of the whole thing going under because the other ones were taking it down and basically tore this family apart.
turns.zh: 其他人则把它当提款机。家里闹得很凶。有个兄弟实际上把整个公司置于倾覆的财务风险之中，因为其他人一直在掏空它，这个家庭基本被撕裂了。

turns.en: So you see a big range of paths. Other businesses employ dozens of people. So there's one family in St. Louis and I asked them at a family gathering.
turns.zh: 所以你会看到大相径庭的多种路径。有些企业雇了很多自家的人。圣路易斯有一家人，我在一次家庭聚会上问他们：

turns.en: I was like, okay, who's the richest kid in your high school to one of my nephews? And they're like, oh, it's the Tracy family. I was like, okay, when does the Tracy family do it?
turns.zh: 你高中里最富有的同学是谁？我有个侄子。他们回答：哦，是 ReTracy 家。我问：那 ReTracy 家是做什么的？

turns.en: They're a food redistributor and the Tracy family, I think that the business is called Dot Foods and they employ something like 57 Tracy family members in the thing.
turns.zh: 做食品再分销的。ReTracy 家族，我记得公司叫 Dot Foods，里面有差不多57个家族成员在这家企业工作。

turns.en: And so there's some cases where it seems to be a bit more harmonious, at least from the outside, there's a range. But one other person we talked to, I think it was interesting, her name's Annette Leroux and she is a sociologist at Penn and she interviewed about a hundred really wealthy families who have all inherited businesses.
turns.zh: 所以有些情况下看起来更和睦一些，至少从外面看是这样，但情况很谱系化。我们还聊过另一个人，我觉得很有意思，她叫 Annette Lareau，是宾夕法尼亚大学的社会学家，访谈了大约一百个真正富有、全部继承家业的家族。

turns.en: And her conclusion, she told me for herself, she said, if I could give my daughter $40 million or zero, I would give her zero because of all the craziness she saw.
turns.zh: 她的结论——她亲口跟我说——她说：如果可以给女儿4000万美元或者给0，她宁愿给0。因为她见识了太多疯狂。

turns.en: I think that's kind of my take on inherited family firms. Those are super interesting stories. Is there like an image in the data of how inheritances affect wealth?
turns.zh: 我想这就是我对继承型家族企业的看法。这些故事真的太有意思了。数据里有没有一幅继承如何影响财富的图景？

turns.en: There's several things. One fact is that it's less prevalent in the U.S. than in some other countries. Some people speculate, that's one of the reasons why the U.S. economy grows faster.
turns.zh: 有好几点。一个事实是：在美国，继承的普遍程度低于一些其他国家。有人推测，这也是美国经济增速更快的原因之一。

turns.en: Warren Buffett had this joke, he was like, if you're gonna select the Olympic team, would you restrict yourself to the sons and daughters of former Olympians or would you go for everybody?
turns.zh: Warren Buffett 有个玩笑：如果选拔奥运代表队，你是只从往届奥运选手的儿子里挑，还是向所有人开放？

turns.en: Some of it is about making sure more people have a shot and you want the best people to rise up and the leadership roles and you get more productivity when you have the right people running things.
turns.zh: 一部分是为了让更多人有上场机会。你要让最优秀的人走上领导岗位，让合适的人掌舵，生产率才会更高。

turns.en: How can business owners successfully exit their business? There's a lot of people who are interested in buying successful businesses now. Some of it is putting yourself in the market for a lot of these hungry business school grads or people who are mid-career who wanna switch and just let it be known that, hey, I have a cash flowing business, that's a good business.
turns.zh: 企业主如何成功地退出自己的企业？现在对收购成功企业感兴趣的人非常多。一部分是把自己放进市场——那么多嗷嗷待哺的商学院毕业生，或者想转型的中年人——让人知道：嘿，我有一门有现金流的好生意。

turns.en: If you really wanna make it work, you can do seller financing so that these people can buy the business in part by using the proceeds of future profits to pay off a loan to you.
turns.zh: 如果真想做成，你可以做卖方融资（seller financing），让买家部分用企业未来的利润来偿还欠你的贷款。

turns.en: To me, I find that very attractive as a potential buyer because then that signals, hey, this person really believes in their business. If they're gonna basically take the promise of future profits from it, that means they believe it's gonna generate future profits.
turns.zh: 作为潜在买家，我觉得这非常有吸引力，因为这传递了一个信号：这个人真的相信自己生意的价值。如果对方愿意用未来利润的承诺来支付，说明他相信未来会有利润。

turns.en: It's not some lemon. That's one key way that I would encourage business owners to think about doing it. And often you can get better terms because it's a valuable thing.
turns.zh: 不是破车一辆。这是我会鼓励企业主去尝试的关键做法之一。而且往往能拿到更好的条款，因为这是有价值的东西。

turns.en: So that's not like it's a free lunch. Can you talk about the benefits and maybe also some of the problems that private equity poses to business owners?
turns.zh: 所以天下没有免费的午餐。能聊聊私募股权（private equity）给企业主带来的好处，也许还有问题吗？

turns.en: Yes, so some of the benefits. So for example, we talked to this doctor and if you think about it from their perspective of a doctor who's their practice bought by private equity, they can do some stuff at scale.
turns.zh: 可以。先说好处。比如我们访谈过一位医生。想想他的处境：诊所被私募股权收购后，很多事可以规模化地做。

turns.en: So if you're running a small practice, there's a bunch of stuff that might not be top of mind. It kind of gets lost in the shuffle, like really being on top of billing and getting paid right away by everybody efficiently.
turns.zh: 如果你经营一家小诊所，很多事不会在你的优先清单上，容易在忙乱中被忽略，比如把账单管理、让所有人高效及时付款这件事真正做扎实。

turns.en: And if you have a private equity firm that has a portfolio of these businesses, they might have some larger scale where they could say, look, this is what's working for our four or five other practices.
turns.zh: 如果是一家私募股权公司把这类诊所组合在一个资产包里，他们有更大规模，可以说：看，这套办法在我们其他四五家诊所行得通。

turns.en: We're gonna put you on this billing provider and then you can get efficiencies that way. So that's the type of thing that I think works pretty well.
turns.zh: 我们把你的账单系统接到这家服务商上，你就能获得这些效率。这类事情我觉得运作得相当好。

turns.en: You can also benefit from knowledge of their other portfolio companies. So say you're navigating some issue with financing or some other strategic issue, there's probably somebody else who's dealt with this or maybe you want some more customers, they can put you in touch with customers.
turns.zh: 你还能受益于他们对其他组合公司的知识。比如你在处理融资或者别的战略问题，很可能别的公司已经遇到过；或者你想要更多客户，他们能帮你牵线。

turns.en: There are a lot of things that they can help with, but there might also be a lot more pressure or there are material pay differences. So this doctor, I remember he complained, he was getting $500,000 less an annual income, which also goes to show you how much doctors make that you could have a delta of 500K and still be making doctor salary because he became an owner rather than getting the salary.
turns.zh: 能帮忙的地方很多，但压力也可能大得多，薪酬上也可能有实质性差异。那位医生我记得抱怨过，他的年收入少了50万美元——这反过来也说明医生挣得多：少了500K 还拿得出医生级别的薪水，因为他从领工资变成了拿股权的老板。

turns.en: So there's some in terms of what the pay looks like as well. So you need to be prepared for that. You might also lose some culture, you might have to make harder decisions about losing employees, maybe you lose control, maybe the business is gonna go in a direction that you didn't wanna take it and that's too bad.
turns.zh: 所以在薪酬面貌上也会有变化，你得有心理准备。你还可能失去一些文化，可能要在裁掉员工上做更艰难的决定，可能失去控制权，生意可能朝你本不想走的方向去，那就太遗憾了。

turns.en: Like you've lost the ability to have that autonomy. And how can private equity be used well by business owners? I think one great use as an exit option to avoid some of those family dynamics that I was talking about before, often they're very hungry for these types of businesses.
turns.zh: 你失去了那份自主性。那企业主怎样才能善用私募股权？我觉得一个绝佳的用法是作为退出选项，避开我说的那些家庭纠葛。这类买家往往非常渴望这样的企业。

turns.en: You know, my first job, I worked at Bain Capital, which was pretty early at this. And I think one of the first, if not the first investments of Bain Capital was Staples.
turns.zh: 我的第一份工作是在 Bain Capital，当时这行还很早期。我想 Bain Capital 最早的投资之一——如果不是最早的话——就是 Staples。

turns.en: This is basically an everywhere millionaire business when it was smaller. It's like they sold office supplies. Mitt Romney really helped grow that business well.
turns.zh: 它在还小的时候，本质上就是一门'无处不在的百万富翁'生意，就是卖办公用品。Mitt Romney 确实帮它把生意做大做好了。

turns.en: And so I think some of the strategic support, some of the financing partnerships bringing customers to people, I think those are all pretty real.
turns.zh: 所以战略支持、融资，以及帮企业对接客户的伙伴关系，我觉得这些都非常实在。能讲讲'隐形整合'（stealth consolidation）的影响吗？

turns.en: Can you talk about the effect of stealth consolidation? Yes, there's a former colleague of mine, Thomas Wolman, who has some great work on stealth consolidation.
turns.zh: 可以。我的一位前同事 Thomas Wolman 有关于隐形整合的很棒的研究。

turns.en: The basic idea is that the benchmark for what flags a review from the FTC is kind of a nominal threshold. So below that threshold, there's a lot of rollups and mergers that happen without review.
turns.zh: 基本思路是：触发 FTC 审查的标准是一个名义金额门槛。在门槛之下，有大量连环并购和合并根本不经过审查。

turns.en: And his basic point is, if you look kind of below the threshold, there's been a ton of consolidation in industries and that's driven up prices and not always been to the benefit of customers.
turns.zh: 他的核心观点是：看门槛以下，各行业已经发生了巨量整合，把价格推了上去，而且并不总是对客户有利。

turns.en: And so if you think about some of the objectives of the Federal Trade Commission should really look below that threshold and maybe consider lowering it because there's been a lot of stealth consolidation.
turns.zh: 所以想想联邦贸易委员会（Federal Trade Commission）的职责，它真应该看门槛以下，也许该考虑把门槛调低，因为隐形整合实在太多。

turns.en: Things like dialysis. He has a bunch of examples that I'm not remembering off the top of my head, but that's the basic idea. So is that like private equity rollups?
turns.zh: 比如透析。他还有不少例子，我一时想不起来了，但思路就是这样。那这是不是就像私募股权的打包整合？

turns.en: They're just buying small private businesses and rolling them up into under one entity? Yes, so sometimes, or it's just not necessarily private equity, just a series of veterinarians who are gonna buy up a bunch of things and all of a sudden they're like, look, we control the local market for vet services.
turns.zh: 就是买下小私营企业、归到一个主体下面？有时候是，但也不一定非得是私募股权。可能就是一群兽医把一大堆诊所买下来，忽然有一天他们说：看，本地兽医服务市场在我们手里了。

turns.en: We're gonna raise prices by 20%. That doesn't have to have anything to do with private equity, just as local consolidation. Interesting. Do you think that affects labor markets too?
turns.zh: 我们要把价格提高20%。这跟私募股权未必有关系，就是本地整合而已。有意思。你觉得这也会影响劳动力市场吗？

turns.en: Yes, so there's some suggestive evidence that when firms have product market power, they can also have some labor market power. That's part of the story for the decline in the labor share.
turns.zh: 会。有一些提示性证据表明，企业在产品市场有定价权时，往往也能获得一定的劳动力市场权力。这是劳动份额下降的故事之一。

turns.en: Now, how big it is, it's hard to quantify all these things on an equal footing, but I think that's part of what's going on. But again, that's very different than the, oh, we need to focus on big tech and the five largest firms that are driving the stock market for breaking them up.
turns.zh: 至于有多大，很难把所有东西放在同一把尺子上量化，但我觉得这是其中一部分。但同样，这跟'要盯着大型科技公司、拆分推动股市的那五家最大公司'是完全不同的问题。

turns.en: This is way more of a local on the ground regional story. It happens like everywhere, where we live in Canada, you see it with dental clinics, dermatology clinics, a lot of medical stuff, veterinarians, like you said, it's happening a lot, just so you can see it.
turns.zh: 这更多是一个本地、在地域层面发生的故事。它无处不在。我们住的加拿大也是这样，你能看到牙科诊所、皮肤科诊所、很多医疗领域，还有你说过的兽医，正在大量发生，一看就能看到。

turns.en: I mean, some of these markets are huge. And so dentists, for example, one of my favorite facts about dentists, if you add up all the revenues of dentists in the United States, it's much larger than the total revenue of the NBA, the NHL, the NFL, MLB, all pro sports teams combined, just dentists make a ton of money.
turns.zh: 我是说，有些这样的市场巨大得很。关于牙科有个我特别喜欢的数据：把美国所有牙医的收入加起来，远超过 NBA、NHL、NFL、MLB 全部职业球队收入之和，就牙医这一个群体就赚翻了。

turns.en: It's just not something you think about, but then when you kind of take a step back, you're like, all right, everybody has teeth. It does make sense.
turns.zh: 这不是你平时会想到的，但退一步看，人人都有牙，确实说得通。

turns.en: And if you see this product market power emerging at the local level can raise prices. They're also pretty effective at fighting political forces to hold prices down.
turns.zh: 当你看到这种产品市场权力在本地层面浮现，它就能提价。而且这些行业在抵制政治力量压价方面也很有一套。

turns.en: So there's some move in the U.S. to include dental services in Medicare, but dentists fought it because they didn't want the price pressure of the U.S. government being able to say, all right, no, no, no, we're not gonna pay that much year after year.
turns.zh: 美国有过把牙科服务纳入 Medicare 的动议，但牙医们奋力抵抗，因为他们不想承受美国政府年复一年说'不行不行，我们不能付那么多'的价格压力。

turns.en: So that's one example of their political clout. You mentioned the great Gatsby earlier. Is the U.S. in a new gilded age? That's a great question.
turns.zh: 你前面提到了《了不起的盖茨比》。美国是否处在又一个镀金时代（Gilded Age）？这是个好问题。

turns.en: So there are certainly some things that would make you think that and many people like Paul Krugman and others have emphasized that we're in a new gilded age.
turns.zh: 确实有一些迹象会让你这么想。Paul Krugman 和很多人都在强调我们身处新镀金时代。

turns.en: So for example, if you look at top income shares, they look just like they did when we first started recording them. The U.S. modern tax started in 1913 until it's a little bit after the gilded age, but we're back even a little above the levels of concentration for the top 0.1% and top 1% that we had at the beginning of the 20th century.
turns.zh: 比如，看最高收入份额，它们和我们刚开始有记录时几乎一模一样。美国现代税制始于1913年，那已经是镀金时代之后不久，但今天前0.1%和前1%的集中程度，甚至比20世纪初还要略高一点。

turns.en: And there's this perception that there's just a small number of Rockefellers and Carnegie types that are dominating the news, but we're quite different in many ways.
turns.zh: 而且有一种印象，觉得就是少数几个 Rockefeller、Carnegie 式的人物在霸占新闻头条，但很多方面我们其实完全不同。

turns.en: Many of these everywhere millionaires are not doing transformational innovation. They're making hot dogs or garage doors or cleaning teeth. So that's pretty different than like building transcontinental railroads or the first type of grand, very capital intensive investments.
turns.zh: 这些'无处不在的百万富翁'里，很多人并没有做变革性创新。他们做热狗、做车库门、给人洗牙。这跟当年建横贯大陆铁路、做第一批超重资本的大投资很不一样。

turns.en: We're in a service economy that's quite different than the economy of the gilded age. And so we like to emphasize that we're kind of in this new age of millionaires where there's just an abundance of wealth and prosperity across America.
turns.zh: 我们身处服务经济，跟镀金时代的经济相当不同。所以我们喜欢强调：我们其实处在一个新的百万富翁时代，财富和繁荣在全美遍地都是。

turns.en: And we're often obsessed with a few billionaires who have been monopolizing attention, but they really do not monopolize wealth in America. We've kind of been touching this.
turns.zh: 我们往往痴迷于少数垄断注意力的亿万富翁，但他们并没有垄断美国的财富。这个我们刚才其实碰到了。

turns.en: Can you talk more about where the class of mainstream millionaires came from? Yes, so there are a couple of reasons why we call them everywhere millionaires.
turns.zh: 能再讲讲这个'主流百万富翁'阶层是怎么来的吗？可以，我们叫他们'无处不在的百万富翁'有几个原因。

turns.en: So you find them in any town in America. In terms of political power, there's also an everywhere millionaire in basically every congressional district.
turns.zh: 在美国任何一个城镇你都能找到他们。就政治影响力而言，基本上每个国会选区也都有一个这样的'无处不在的百万富翁'。

turns.en: And so when you think about who is the senator or who is the member of Congress or who plays golf with the member of Congress, who employs a lot of people in the district.
turns.zh: 想想参议员是谁、国会议员是谁、跟国会议员打高尔夫的是谁、在选区里雇了大量工人的是谁。

turns.en: Think about all the sales tax revenues. So auto dealers, for example, employ something like 10% of retail employment. They bring in something like 20% of state sales taxes.
turns.zh: 再想想销售税。比如汽车经销商雇用了大约10%的零售就业，贡献了各州大约20%的销售税。

turns.en: These are pretty important people from the perspective of the governor, the congressperson or the mayor. It's a lot of jobs. It's a lot of money.
turns.zh: 从州长、国会议员、市长的角度看，这些人相当重要。那是大量的工作岗位，大量的钱。

turns.en: And they have a lot of influence as a result of that. It's pretty different than Elon Musk who donated a ton of money in elections and got a doge.
turns.zh: 因此他们也有很大的影响力。这跟 Elon Musk 很不一样——他捐款巨多，还得了个 DOGE。

turns.en: But when you look at what actually happened in terms of concrete policy, so take one big beautiful bill act. Elon Musk was a loser in that he lost a lot of clean energy credits.
turns.zh: 但看具体政策实际怎么落地的，就拿那部'大而美法案'（One Big Beautiful Bill Act）来说，Elon Musk 其实是输的那个：他失去了大量清洁能源抵免。

turns.en: The EV incentives were cut and then kind of everywhere millionaire auto dealer got 7% deduction on their taxes. So from 37 to 30 preserved, they got a workaround from some caps on state taxes.
turns.zh: 电动车激励被砍了，而'无处不在的百万富翁'里的汽车经销商保住了7%的税收抵扣，从37%降到30%的降幅被豁免，还找到了州税上限的绕道办法。

turns.en: They got a special new deduction where if you buy a new car, you can deduct from your taxes the loan you took out to buy it. I think when you actually look at the details of what happens, you should be focusing much more on this group of people because they're influence rivals that of the much more in the news billionaires that some people are very worried about.
turns.zh: 他们还拿到一项新的特殊抵扣：买新车可以把为此申请的贷款从税里扣掉。我觉得真看细节的话，大家应该更关注这一群人，因为他们的影响力，堪比那些更上新闻、让很多人忧心忡忡的亿万富翁。

turns.en: I'm so interested to think about why this is an interesting topic for a book. You don't hear about those people or people don't worry about them.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，为什么这能成为一个有意思的书题。你平时根本听不到这些人，人们也不担心他们。

turns.en: People worry about, like you said, Elon Musk. For a good reason, but at the same time, once you see it, you kind of see it everywhere. So one of our hopes in writing the book is that I mean, one is to inspire people because there are some really inspirational stories about business owners who rise from the bottom to the top and bring a lot of good people with them.
turns.zh: 人们担心的是——像你刚才说的——Elon Musk，这有道理。但同一时间，这种东西一旦你看见了，就到处都看得见。我们写这本书有一个愿望，就是希望能激励人，因为确实有些企业主从底层爬到顶层、还带着一大群好人一起向上的励志故事。

turns.en: And I think we should have more millionaires in America. We should have more people who have a shot at becoming millionaires. But also we should be quite aware of how powerful this group can also be.
turns.zh: 我觉得美国应该有更多百万富翁，应该有更多有机会成为百万富翁的人。但同时，我们也要清醒地知道这群人可以有多大的力量。

turns.en: Very careful about things that are kind of, we need to make sure small business with a little guy is okay because that's been the Trojan horse that's led to a lot of problems.
turns.zh: 对那些打着'要照顾小企业、照顾小人物'旗号的东西要非常小心，因为那一直是引出很多问题的特洛伊木马。

turns.en: Once you kind of recognize this, you see it everywhere in political debates. If you kind of follow the details of how some things shake out.
turns.zh: 一旦你认出了这套东西，在政治辩论里就会到处看到它，只要你跟着细节看事情最后怎么落地。

turns.en: How important are interest rates in driving increases in wealth? They're central. They're one of the most important macro factors. When rates came down at the great moderation after Paul Volcker, that was the first order cause of a lot of the boom in the stock market and in private business valuations.
turns.zh: 利率在推动财富增长中有多重要？它们是核心，是最重要的宏观因素之一。Paul Volcker 之后、'大缓和'期间利率下行，是股市和私营企业估值繁荣的第一因。

turns.en: Are there implications of that? One thing is when you think about what's really going on with top wealth, you need to make a distinction of flows versus stocks.
turns.zh: 那有什么含义吗？有一件事：要想明白顶级财富上真正发生了什么，得区分流量和存量。

turns.en: And the flows might not have changed that much, but the stocks change a lot if you're changing the discount rate for future cash flows. So when you see that, oh, wealth doubled, that doesn't necessarily mean that the annual profits doubled from the perspective of business owners.
turns.zh: 流量可能变化并不大，但只要给未来现金流换一个折现率，存量就会剧烈变化。所以看到'财富翻了一倍'，从企业主角度看，未必是年利润翻了一倍。

turns.en: They may be like, look, my flows are the same. I don't feel as rich as you say I am on paper. So that's one thing that you might get as an upshot of interest rates movements causing a lot of the rise in wealth accumulation.
turns.zh: 他们可能会说：看，我的流量没变，我并没有像你说我那么有钱——那只是纸面上的。利率变动推动了大量财富账面增长，你得到的结论可能就是这一点。

turns.en: How can more people be helped to climb the ladder of financial success? Yeah, so I think some is really getting a lot of people early labor market experience that puts them on a path to be in these more entrepreneurial sectors.
turns.zh: 怎样才能帮更多人登上财务成功的阶梯？我觉得一部分是让更多人尽早获得劳动力市场经验，把他们放进这些更有创业氛围的行业。

turns.en: That is one quite important thing that we should consider how to do that better because it does seem like exposure, if you're, as we were talking about before, if your parents are business owners, you're much more likely to become a business on yourself.
turns.zh: 这是件相当重要、我们应该研究怎么做得更好的事，因为接触（exposure）看起来确实关键——就像我们刚才说的，如果父母是企业主，你自己成为企业主的概率大得多。

turns.en: So exposure to this type of experience, I think is quite key. So more apprenticeship type opportunities and a more thoughtful cultivation of upward paths and careers that aren't necessarily in the conventional study hard, go to a good college, go to a name brand firm and earn a salary.
turns.zh: 所以这类经历的接触非常关键。更多的学徒式机会，更有心地把向上的职业路径铺出来，而不一定是'好好学习、考好大学、进名牌公司、拿工资'那条老路。

turns.en: Thinking about these alternative paths, I think is a way to do that. And how can would be entrepreneurs reduce their risks and boost their odds of success?
turns.zh: 思考这些替代路径，我觉得就是一个办法。那么，想创业的人怎样降低风险、提高成功概率？

turns.en: There's this pretty interesting study out of Harvard Business School. The way Harvard Business School is set up, and my co-author, Eric Zweck, went there, so I can learn some of these fun stories from him.
turns.zh: 哈佛商学院有个很有意思的研究。HBS 的建制是按'教学小组'（section）分的——我的合著者 Eric Zwick 就是那里的，这些有趣的故事我也是从他那儿听来的。

turns.en: It's set up in sections. So you kind of have this small group of people that you kind of take everything with. They looked at entrepreneurs who were placing sections, which are the allocations random.
turns.zh: 每个人有一个固定的小组，所有课程都跟这个小组一起上。研究者看的是创业者如何被分配到不同的小组，而这种分配是随机的。

turns.en: Some of them were in sections where someone else had entrepreneurial experience, and some were in groups that didn't have any people with former experience.
turns.zh: 有些人的小组里恰好有做过创业的人，有些人的组里完全没有任何有创业经历的人。

turns.en: And what you found is that people who are in sections with somebody with experience, they're much less likely to start something, but conditional on starting it, they're much more likely to succeed.
turns.zh: 结果发现：分在有过来人所在小组里的人，自己出来创业的可能性更低，可一旦真去创业，成功率却高得多。

turns.en: And so it seemed like talking to people who've done this type of thing before and really vetting ideas is an important way to achieve what you asked of having entrepreneurs have less risk and more success.
turns.zh: 所以看起来，跟干过这事的人聊、把点子好好掂量掂量，正是实现你说的那个目标——让创业者风险更小、成功更多——的重要途径。

turns.en: So it's basically getting exposure to people who have done this before is one thing that seems to work. What do you think of some of the practical steps that could be taken in the US to reduce inequality, but preserve the ability of business owners to hire and fire workers?
turns.zh: 说到底，接触做过这件事的人，看起来就是管用的一招。对于美国可以在减少不平等的同时、又保住企业主雇用和解雇工人的能力的一些实操步骤，你怎么看？

turns.en: So first, this book is not a policy book. We very actively tried not to do that. I think about these things a lot, but I'll just rattle off a few.
turns.zh: 首先，这本书不是政策书，我们非常刻意地避免写政策。这些问题我想了很多，但我可以随口说几条。

turns.en: So one, we talked about health insurance and healthcare reform. Another is just basically resetting the tax code back to what it was in 1997.
turns.zh: 一条是我们谈过的健康保险和医疗改革。另一条基本就是把税法重置回1997年的样子。

turns.en: We jokingly call it party like it's 1997. Growth was very high then. We had surplus is not deficits and we'd raised trillions of dollars to go back to that era.
turns.zh: 我们开玩笑说叫'像1997年那样嗨'。那时候增长很高，财政是盈余不是赤字，我们可以加回数万亿美元税收、回到那个年代。

turns.en: Some of the cuts that we've had just have not been that effective in generating new employment and investment. And so we think some reset is appropriate, mostly on the individual side.
turns.zh: 这些年的一些减税在创造新就业和投资方面并没有那么有效。所以我们认为做些重置是合适的，主要是在个人税这一侧。

turns.en: Another is that we haven't raised the minimum wage in decades. It doesn't have to be astronomically high, but if just set what it was with inflation is a reasonable benchmark and there's some pretty good empirical work looking at the effects on businesses and what actually happens.
turns.zh: 还有一条是最低工资几十年没涨了。不一定要涨到天上去，只要按通胀把当年的水平找回来就是个合理的基准，而且已有一些不错的实证研究在看对企业的影响和实际结果。

turns.en: A lot of it kind of gets passed through consumers or the owners eat it. So if you're thinking about that question about the labor share and some of the dynamics, I think that would do some work to offset those dynamics a little bit without having a major drag on productivity and employment and investments.
turns.zh: 很大一部分要么转嫁给消费者，要么由所有者消化。所以想想你之前关于劳动份额的那些动态，我认为这能在不重挫生产率、就业和投资的前提下，稍微对冲一下那些趋势。

turns.en: I do think when people talk about policy solutions, they really should be quite cautious about shrinking the pie. And that's something I care quite a bit about.
turns.zh: 我的确认为，人们谈论政策方案时，对'缩小蛋糕'必须非常谨慎。这一点我非常在意。

turns.en: So we have some work, for example, showing parts of the 2017 tax reform really stimulated a lot of investment. I do think we need to think about outcomes when we're talking about policy.
turns.zh: 比如我们有些研究显示，2017年税改的部分内容确实刺激了大量投资。谈政策时，我认为必须以结果为导向。

turns.en: And so like there's some things that work quite well and we need to focus our resources on that. And the stuff that doesn't work, we really need to question.
turns.zh: 有些做法相当有效，我们要把资源集中到那里；对没效果的做法，真要好好打问号。

turns.en: And the stuff that doesn't work as well or this like 7% deduction for business owners that cost a trillion dollars that was preserved in the 2025 bill.
turns.zh: 包括效果不佳的那些——比如给企业主的这7%的抵扣，花了上万亿美元，还在2025年的法案里被保留下来。

turns.en: Like that's the type of thing we can't afford right now. But some of the investment incentives did seem to be more effective. It's why I would keep those.
turns.zh: 这种开支眼下我们真负担不起。倒是那些投资激励看起来更有效，所以我倾向于保留它们。

turns.en: Really interesting. Final question for you, Owen. How do you define success in your life? There's a couple of different dimensions. One is having a happy and healthy family.
turns.zh: 真有意思。Owen，最后一个问题：你如何定义自己人生里的成功？有好几个维度。一个是拥有幸福健康的家庭。

turns.en: I'm blessed with three young kids and a wife. We have three, they're all under five. And so it's pretty chaotic at the moment. So sleep, I basically have my answers and just been hours of sleep is my current measure of happiness.
turns.zh: 我很幸运，有三个小孩和一位太太，三个孩子都还不满五岁，所以家里现在相当鸡飞狗跳。睡眠基本就是我现在衡量幸福的指标——睡了几个小时。

turns.en: No, but working in a profession where I can try to work on things that I'm interested in and let more people know about ways that we can make the economy work better and have policy work better and give people a shot.
turns.zh: 不开玩笑，能在一个可以研究自己感兴趣的课题的职业里工作，让更多人知道怎样让经济更好、政策更好、让更多人有机会，这本身就很珍贵。

turns.en: Cause I do think learning about some of these stories is pretty inspiring. And so I'd like more people to be able to prosper in their lives.
turns.zh: 因为我确实觉得，了解这些故事挺励志的。我希望更多人能让自己的人生过得好。

turns.en: And so having a healthy family, a healthy and exciting job where you can help other people, I think are two measures of success that I think about.
turns.zh: 所以，家庭健康，工作既有活力又有意义、还能帮到别人——我觉得这就是我心中成功的两条标准。

turns.en: Love it. This is a great conversation. Congratulations on your book and this research. It's fascinating. Thank you so much. You'll sleep eventually, don't worry.
turns.zh: 太喜欢了。这是一场精彩的对话。恭喜你的书和这些研究，太迷人了。非常感谢。总会睡整觉的，别担心。

turns.en: Yeah. I've got four kids under 11 now. Oh, wow. At one point I did have three kids under five. I didn't sleep either, but you'll sleep one day.
turns.zh: 是的。我现在有四个11岁以下的孩子。哇。我曾经也有三个五岁以下的，那阵子我也没怎么睡过，但你总有一天会睡着的。

turns.en: I can look forward to that. Awesome. Well, thank you all so much for having me. It's been a real pleasure talking to you. Love it. Take care.
turns.zh: 我可以盼着那天了。太好了。非常感谢你们邀请我，跟你们聊天真的是荣幸。喜欢你们。再见。

turns.en: Thanks, Owen. You know, Ben, it's gotta be 30 plus years ago where we were presented in our office. This is way back in the old mutual fund days.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Owen。你知道吗，Ben，那得是三十多年前了，我们在办公室里收到一本书——那可是老共同基金时代的陈年往事了——

turns.en: The book called The Millionaire Next Door. And that was my first introduction to the thinking around like, who is the average millionaire out there?
