turns.zh: 就是《邻家的百万富翁》（The Millionaire Next Door）。那是我第一次接触到'百万富翁到底是什么人'这类思考。

turns.en: And what do they do? Where did the wealth come from? And what are their habits? And where do they drive? And where do they eat? And how do they spend?
turns.zh: 他们是干什么的？财富从哪里来？他们有什么习惯？开什么车？在哪儿吃饭？怎么花钱？

turns.en: And I remember finding that book so fascinating. Of course, it was presented to us as a way to help us connect and find our potential future clients.
turns.zh: 我记得那本书当时让我着迷。当然，它被推荐给我们，是作为一种帮我们建立人脉、找到未来潜在客户的工具。

turns.en: But I can remember that day like yesterday being presented with that book by I think it's Dr. Tom Stanley was either the author or co-author of that book.
turns.zh: 但那天我至今历历在目：有人把这本书递给我，作者或合著者我记得是 Dr. Tom Stanley。

turns.en: And then to have this conversation today with Owen, it's like, wow, just be right back in time. But with this unbelievably modern set of data.
turns.zh: 而今天又能和 Owen 有这样一场对话，简直像是时光倒流，只是配上了这套令人难以置信的现代数据。

turns.en: He took the premise of that book and gave it an economist's treatment. And as he talks about, they got their hands on data that just nobody else has had before.
turns.zh: 他把那本书的前提用经济学家的方式重新做了一遍。而且像他说的，他们拿到了别人从没有过的数据。

turns.en: And so they're able to build that incredible profile of what typical millionaire looks like. And then I loved combining the data work they did, the empirical work they did with conversations, with the everyday millionaires that they identified to understand all that stuff.
turns.zh: 所以他们才能勾勒出典型百万富翁令人惊叹的全貌。我还特别喜欢他们把数据工作、实证工作，与和那些被识别出来的'邻家百万富翁'本人的对话结合起来，去理解这些东西。

turns.en: Like about how they spend their money and how they spend their time, who they are. I love the hustle part. Maybe that's cause I like to work a lot too, but just the idea that they're just regular people that work really hard, work a lot, don't like to stop working, don't necessarily spend lavishly.
turns.zh: 比如他们怎么花钱、怎么安排时间、他们是谁。我喜欢那种'埋头苦干'的部分。可能因为我也爱工作，就觉得他们其实只是特别努力的普通人：工作很久、不想停下来、也不一定挥金如土——

turns.en: But as he talked about, some do. Some do. And some have very conservative lifestyles. Through most of their working lives. And at the end, they really go and live it up.
turns.zh: 不过像他说的，也有挥金的。确实有。也有些人几乎整个职业生涯都过得很节俭，到人生后段才真正开始享受。

turns.en: It's interesting, like in our roles, we get front row seat to seeing how people with some pretty good savings, how they do spend their money.
turns.zh: 很有意思。以我们的角色，前排看得到那些攒下可观储蓄的人到底怎么花钱。

turns.en: But what I think we find more interesting is how they earned their money. And we have so many examples of businesses where you just go, huh, I never even knew that thing, that need existed.
turns.zh: 但我们觉得更有意思的，往往是他们怎么赚到钱。我们有太多例子，是那种你会说'咦，我都不知道世界上还有这种东西、这种需求'的生意。

turns.en: They built these unbelievable enterprises completely under the radar. And we have many of those cases. Yeah, we've got some technology people that have hit it there.
turns.zh: 他们在完全低调的情况下建起了了不起的企业。这样的案例我们有很多。对，也有些是做科技赚到钱的。

turns.en: But to see these businesses, that you had no idea existed at all. Some of those professionals, that he talked about dentists, doctors, lawyers, professionals, to your point, Cam, we have so many interesting cases where the client has a business that like you said, you didn't even know that was a thing that existed.
turns.zh: 可看到那些你原本完全不知道存在的企业——就像他说的那些专业人士，牙医、医生、律师们——Cam，正如你说的，我们有不少这样的有趣案例：客户的生意是你压根不知道还能有这种行当的。

turns.en: But of course it does. Someone's got to do that super niche or not fun to do thing. As no one talked about there, the people that do those things can make a whole whack of money doing it.
turns.zh: 但行当当然存在。总得有人去做那些超冷门、或者没人愿意干的活儿。就像刚才说的，做这些事的人能赚到一大笔钱。

turns.en: A little bit more on Owen, we gave him a very brief introduction, but he is a professor of economics and public affairs at Princeton, jointly appointed in the economics department in the School of Public and International Affairs.
turns.zh: 再多介绍一点 Owen。刚才只给了很简短的介绍，但他是普林斯顿大学经济学与公共事务教授，同时在经济系和国际公共事务学院联合任职。

turns.en: Prior to Princeton, he was an assistant professor at Chicago Booth, where we've had many guests from. He's also a staff economist at the Council of Economic Advisors and an analyst at Bain Capital, which he did mention.
turns.zh: 去普林斯顿之前，他是芝加哥大学 Booth 商学院的助理教授——我们节目请过很多来自 Booth 的嘉宾。他还是总统经济顾问委员会（Council of Economic Advisers）的研究经济学家，也做过 Bain Capital 的分析员，这个他刚才也提到了。

turns.en: He's got his PhD from UC Berkeley. Super interesting conversation. He's got a book, and of course we were talking about, we get a lot of folks reaching out, wanting to talk about their books, and we don't usually have them on because they're not usually economists with really data-driven things to talk about.
turns.zh: 他在 UC Berkeley 拿到博士学位。一场特别有意思的对话。他出了书，就是我们刚才聊的那种——我们经常收到很多人自荐想聊他们的书，我们一般不请，因为他们通常不是真正拿数据说话的经济学家。

turns.en: But when I saw this one come in, I took a quick flip through it and it was pretty obvious it would be an interesting conversation, which I think it was.
turns.zh: 但看到这本找上门时，我快速翻了翻，就很明显这会是一场有意思的对话——我觉得也确实是。

turns.en: I agree. Anything else Ben, you want to add? I'm curious in your thoughts Cameron, on just the value of entrepreneurship. You've lived that life, you're still living it on a different side of it now.
turns.zh: 同意。Ben，还有什么要补充的吗？Cameron，我其实很好奇你对创业精神的价值怎么看。你亲身经历过那种生活，现在正从另一面继续经历着。

turns.en: You talked about that the decades of grinding. This is something, you know, Seinfeld talks about a lot. It's like, to find something that most people would find drudgery that you just love doing, you keep working at that craft for years and years.
turns.zh: 你刚才谈到几十年如一日地苦干。这也是 Seinfeld 常聊的点：找到一件大多数人觉得是苦差事、你却乐在其中的事，然后在这个手艺上年复一年地打磨。

turns.en: As I found myself thinking like, like back on 35 years of doing this, it's just unbelievable to me that, A, I did it 30 years in PWL alone. And to have loved all of it, it's just that continual grind through years.
turns.zh: 我自己回想，做这行35年了，真的难以置信：单是在 PWL 就干了30年，而且我全都乐在其中。就是长年累月不间断的耕耘。

turns.en: You combine with that, some of the habits that David Booth talked about when he joined us, just the compounding effect of working at a craft and then trying to squirrel some money away to go along.
turns.zh: 再叠加 David Booth 上次来节目时讲的那些习惯：在一门手艺上滚复利的雪球，同时想法子攒下一些钱一起滚。

turns.en: It's just a lifelong pursuit. Is it entrepreneurship? I guess so, but it's like, to find something you love doing that others might not want to do.
turns.zh: 这是一辈子的事。这算创业吗？我想算吧。但关键是，找到一件你热爱、而别人可能不愿干的事。

turns.en: It's just pretty cool to be lucky enough to have found this career. I think in your case, it's definitely been entrepreneurship. But even when we met 13 or so years ago, you were not in the same position that you were still grinding.
turns.zh: 能有幸找到这份职业，真的挺酷的。我觉得对你来说，这确确实实是创业。可哪怕在我们相识的那十三年前，你还远不是今天的位置——你那时还在埋头苦干。

turns.en: Like you were still in the middle of the grind. It's just so interesting to think about the compounding effects that you don't see. When we met, it was not obvious that you were building the business that we ended up building.
turns.zh: 你正处在苦干的中间。想想那些你当时看不见的复利效应，真是太有意思了。我们认识时，完全看不出你在打造我们后来做成的那家企业。

turns.en: You had your head down, you were grinding, you kept grinding, and then it almost seems like, and it's not in the like there, but it almost seems like all of a sudden, it was this incredible business.
turns.zh: 你低着头干、拼了命干、一直干。然后几乎像是一夜之间——当然不是一夜之间——它突然就成了一家了不起的公司。

turns.en: But that's just the long-term effect of compounding and grinding and keeping your head down and working your butt off. Some luck in making good decisions.
turns.zh: 但那就是复利的长期效应：苦干、埋头、拼尽全力，再加上做对了些决定的运气。

turns.en: It's interesting, as we talked about this last week, we had our annual sum that were 150 plus or minus of us were in one place. It was one thing to look back 13 years when it was a handful of us and it was all our individual hustle.
turns.zh: 有意思。就像我们上周说的，我们开了年度大会，150人上下聚在一堂。回望十三年前还是只有几个人的小团队，全靠各自打拼。

turns.en: It sounds like entrepreneurship is the ability to keep up that vision as you keep growing and empower a team to keep up, I'm talking about the flywheel, it's to keep up what was started 30 plus years ago.
turns.zh: 听起来，创业精神就是随着企业不断成长，依然守得住那份愿景，并让团队跟上——我说的就是这个飞轮：把三十多年前开始的事情延续下去。

turns.en: But to go from like a handful of people to like a ballroom full of people, it's a whole different game. What we're doing is incredible and desperately needed by so many people, what we represent, you know, the simple concept of market's work and planning really matters.
turns.zh: 可从几个人到一个舞厅坐满人，完全是另一种打法。我们在做的事情了不起，又是那么多人迫切需要的——我们所代表的，就是'市场有效、规划重要'这个简单的理念。

turns.en: It's so desperately needed. The mission is clear, but it's to take that into, empower and energize and give the vision to 150 people to hopefully have 300 people in the near future.
turns.zh: 它太被需要了。使命很清楚，难的是把它带到150人那里，让他们有力量、有能量、有共同愿景，并且很快扩展到300人。

turns.en: Had no idea this was at all possible when you and I first met. You think back, I mean, and we're kind of riffing a different stuff here, but back in the day before you even joined, we used to have an annual client seminar.
turns.zh: 你我刚认识的时候，根本不知道这一切有可能发生。回想起来——我们在这儿即兴闲聊——早在你还没加入的时候，我们就办年度客户研讨会。

turns.en: We get 80 people out, 100 people out, and it was expensive and there was a lot of hustle. And we thought that was pretty good. And now how many people a month are listening to this and to your YouTube channel?
turns.zh: 来80人、100人，花费不菲，费劲不小，我们当时觉得挺好了。现在呢，每个月有多少人在听这期节目，还有你的 YouTube 频道？

turns.en: It's in the hundreds of thousands, if not in the millions. It's just a whole different scale, same basic belief system. Just the scale of what you can create by keeping your head down that compounding effect for years and decades, it's incredible.
turns.zh: 数十万计，搞不好上百万。完全是另一个量级，可基本的信念体系一模一样。就靠埋头苦干，让复利在多年、几十年间滚动，你能创造出的规模不可思议。

turns.en: Keep your head down, try and stuff, some luck for sure, but it's a silent compounding. You're grinding, you're doing stuff, and then all of a sudden you have a viable, successful business.
turns.zh: 埋头苦干、不停尝试，肯定有运气成分，但那是无声的复利。你苦干、你做事，忽然有一天，手里就有了一家站得住、做得成的生意。

turns.en: And you keep grinding and compounding, but it's really, as I always say, it's the unintended outcomes, the unintended consequences, the stuff that happens, the accidental meeting, the accidental whatever that might happen, that you say, wow, you couldn't have planned for that, but if you weren't grinding and had your head down and opened up these opportunities, that never would have happened.
turns.zh: 然后你继续苦干、继续复利。但真的，就像我常说的，成事的是那些无心插柳的结果、意外的际遇——那次偶然的会面、那次偶然的什么。你会说：哇，这根本计划不出来，可如果你没有在苦干、没有沉下心、没有给自己敞开机会，它永远不会发生。

turns.en: But as we said last week, 30 years, and we're just getting started. So interesting to think about. We talked a little bit about the consolidation that everyone talked about, super interesting, but also just people know I've done a bunch of house renovation type stuff, and you look at the people in trades who are scaling businesses.
turns.zh: 不过就像我们上周说的，30年，我们才刚起步。想想真有意思。我们聊了一点大家常说的整合，超级有意思。另外大家都知道，我自己动手搞过不少房屋翻新，你看看建筑手艺行业里那些把生意做成规模的人——

turns.en: There are individual tradespeople that make a good living, whatever, but then there are others who are scaling their business, taking on lots of clients, hiring the right people to help them build a business, and they can turn into really, really successful businesses really quickly, but they're not the kind of thing that people think about when they think about how do you get wealthy.
turns.zh: 单个的手艺人能挣份不错的收入，但另一些人把生意做大：接大量客户、招对人帮自己建公司，很快就能变成非常成功的企业。只是大家想到'怎么变富'的时候，不会想到这类生意。

turns.en: I agree. Great message from Alvin, as we said already, his ability to take data to that great message is something that I don't think has been done before, as he talked about.
turns.zh: 同意。Owen 传递的信息很棒，正如我们说的，他把数据变成那样精彩信息的能力，我觉得以前没人做到过——他自己也提到了。
